FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

January is the month when all those who *have it within their power, do migrate to summer regions ; still the great majority of womankind have perforce to remain at home and cheer and encourage their drooping spirits through the dull days, by acquiring marvellous bargains at the sales. Now is the time, when after the rush of gaieties are over, and people begin to settle down again to humdrum every-day life, it is wise to consider future exigencies, and to lay in a stock of oddments of ribbon, lace, chiffon, silk or satin; while for those Who have money to spare there are model gowns which can be purchased at very much less than their original price. At the January sales we can really pick up bargains such as will carry us through the rest of the winter, provided we g% early and select wisely. There are short lengths of' crepe de chine or Oriental satin, in exquisite colourings which are really well worth investing as they can be transformed by clever fingers intu all sorts

He mounted his horse and galloped on towards the hunt, and I hastened to finish my mission and to. get back to the Chase. When I entered the studio after lunch Mr. Gerald was with his mother. Lady Isabella had undoubtedly been crying, but, nevertheless, she looked bright and .happy, and I took no notice and asked no questions. Mr. Gerald retained his seat beside his mother, which was _always a hint that he did not want me to take his place; so when I had delivered my message I went away again, down to the library to finish the cataloguing which Irma had interrupted the day before. I worked busily there until the dusk began to fall. It fell early in the library, for the window was shadowed by a fine cedar that Sir George would not cut down. I was putting aside my work, and wondering if Mr. Gerald were still with his mother —for I thought he would certainly have let me know if she -.fore alone—when the light was still further obscured by a form at the window. I looked up, and there was Irma pressing her face against the glass. She was in walking costume, so she must have left the hunt early, and been home to change her habit. I was surprised to see her, for She rarely got- home on a hunt-day until tea- time. I raised the window, and she stepped in. "I thought I might find you here, Rachel," she said. "I don't want anyone else in the house to
see me.". .."How solemn you are, Irma!" I exclaimed. "What is the matter? " "Life is solemn," she replied, "and full of deceit: No one is to be trusted. All men are liars--and women. too, I believe."

The hopeless words, coming from her rosy young lips in that winning drawl, were inexpressibly touching.. I put my arm round her,and drew her ,to the thick rug, and stirred the fire to a bright blaze. But she put my arm away.. "I wonder you can look at, me, Rachel." "Why should I not look at you? " "I wish you hadn't, given me those diamonds, Rachel .; then I couM quarrel with you." "Yon can send them back, and quarrel with me afterwards, Irma." . "I don't want to send them back, but I am very disappointed in you, Rachel. You have destroyed my belief for ever. / shall never, never believe in anyone again. How long have you known Mr. Ward, Rachel? ", Here was the explanation of her blighted life! In a moment I understoo'd it all. Se had seen Paul walking with me in the lane. Could it be that she was jealous? y heart leaped with joy at

div.head: ART TOILE
div.p: ART TOILE

of dainty garments from a teagown to an abbreviated tea jacket. Lace of course is always useful, whether in the form of piece lace, which is useful for making blouse yokes or transparent sleeves ; to late edging whose uses are so numerous as to defy enumeration. Yards of passementerie, or any handsome trimming are also sure to come in useful later on for applique on gowns or blouses. The smart toilette depicted is of a simple style and yet if properly made, is at once fash- ionable and stylish. It is made in this instance of black cloth, the coat being of the Newmarket ordar. With it is worn a wide shaped black toque trimmed with a few touches of white and a smart ermine tie and muff, the latter lined with white silk. The girl who wore the toilette described was possessc.d of a slim, yet well rounded 'figure, and had a clear but softly coloured complexion and fair hair slightly tinged with red. A bunch of fresh sweet scented violets tucked into the breast- of her coat and she presented a most charming tout ensemble mode even among a crowd of mach more gor- geously arrayed companions. Women are too apt to forget that simplicity is really the

div.head: PRETTY BLOUSE.
div.p: A PRETTY BLOUSE.
dominant feature in the scheme of a really tastefully dressed woman, and it is exceedingly unwise for most to affect any extravagancies of fashion.

It is only the leaders of the sartorial world who can afford to carry their whims and fancies to "extremes, and we are wise if only a hint of the most prominent modes is to be found expressed in the style of our gowns or headgear. Extremes of all sorts must be eschewed by all sensible women of the middle classes.

The pretty blouse sketched is for morning wear, and is made of the new silk flannel, a really delightful material resembling somewhat Roman satin, only being much finer and more supple. The colour is pale blue and the neck is finished by one of the fashionable silk stock ties. This material which is one of this season's novelties, is made only in soft and delicate ,shades and looks very lovely when trimmed with lace and guipure. _

Another material which is delightful for morning skirts, is pannette. This has a soft silky surface and a woolly back, and also appears at its best when adorned by one ,or tare -touches of lace of one kind or another.

div.p: A WINTER HAT.

Viyella of course is also much in evidence owing greatly to the lovely tones of colour in which it can be got, and also because of its excellent washing qualities, as it neither shrinks nor ,fades. I saw a very smart blouse of silk flannel which was made with a simulated bolero which was secured at the breast and again at the waist by a rosette of narrow black velvet ribbon. The opening down the front was filled in by some lace. The Parisieunes are at present very fond of wearing blouses of white or very pale coloured chiffon or net underneath their fur coats; the contrast of the fur and the fragile blouse material being undoubtedly good. I heard someone well known in the world of dress, remark it takes quite a clever English- woman now-a-days to get an ugly hat," so that much credit is evidently due to the taste of our milliners. There is however no fault to be found with the smart hat depicted. It is of fur, the low and rather flat crown is swathed round with white tulle over which is lightly arranged a piece of real lace caught here and there with tiny brilliant headed pins. In front a white aigrette is held in place by. a small brilliant buckle, while under the brim at the left side covering the bandeau a bunch of shaded Parma violets is arranged. There are many of these fur toques or hats to be seen on. all sides, but it is not given to all to achieve the success of this modfl. Grey squirrel fur is very fashionable this season, but it certainly needs some touch of bright colour to render it becoming.

The latest veils (which were first produced for the benefit of the motorists, and which have been warmly welcomed by all women whose skins are easily affeated by cold winds), are of white chiffon, patterned over with black chenille spots, or a spider's web like pattern, laid over the white chiffon. When properly adjusted, and to do so is no easy task, these veils are undoubtedly smart looking.

div.p: Councillor Bennett and the Charges
Against the Council.

A very pleasant function, which afforded evidence of the pride with which many former scholars at the Warrington Blue Coat School look back upon their connection With the institution, and of the bond of friendship which exists between "Old Blues," took place at the Lion Hotel on Monday evening when the members of the Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society held their annual dinner. The society dates its foundation from the year 1855 and its objects are worthy of the warmest commendation and support. After scholars have left the Blue Coat School, the society continues to take, as it were, a perental interest in them, and sees that nothing shall be lacking to enable them to obtain a good start in life and to make the best use of the instruction imparted to them. There was a large assembly at Monday evening's dinner, the attendance including many who have only very recently become entitled to call themselves "Old Blues." On the other hand there were present,gentlemen who were scholars in the days gone by and have now beconie well-known and highly esteemed in commercial circles in the town. In addition to those who are con- nected with the school a number of invited gu estswere present. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. Rose, the respected head master who has nearly completed his twenty-first year of service in that office, and amongst others present were the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton and H. R. Wild, Councillors Bennett andForshaw,Mesars. Roger C. Parr, W. Owen, A. Neil, Dr. Braide, W. H. J. Jenkins, R. Crompton, W. Dannett, Mitchell (Liverpool), J. O'Neill (Liverpool), F. Rose, T. Armstrong and F. Short (secretary of the society). An excellent dinner was served, the catering of Mrs. Gilbert giving every satis- faction. After the repast, the usual toast list was gone through. The SECRETARY said he had received letters of apology for non-attendance from the Mayor,the Rector, essrs. F. Monks, C. M. Merchant (Bury), Gilbert, epherd and James Tinsley. The loyal toasts were honoured on the proposition of he CHAIRMAN. THE WORKING OF THE.' EDUCATION ACT

div.head: SUGGESTION TO THE NEW AUTHORITY
div.p: A SUGGESTION TO THE NEW AUTHORITY

Mr. W. OWEN proposed "The Church and Ministers of all Denominations," and after an allusion to the late Primate, spoke in eulogistic terms of the work of the clergy and ministers in Warrington. Continuing he said the Education Act would come into force on March 26th and unless the clergy and ministers put their shoulders together the Act was not going to be a suc- cess. If the ministers and clergy would put their heads, their shoulders and their hearts into the work, the Education Bill of 1902 would be the Education Act of the future and would do good to the present generation and to all who succeeded them. The toast was heartily honoured, In responding, the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said the Mlle Coat School was a standing memorial of the inter- est which had been taken in the past by the Church in educational matters. It took them hack to a period when the only educational agencies in the country were those which were carried on under the auspices of the Church. That the , work which the church did at that time was done well, ; was sufficiently certified by the fact that those institu- tions still survived and flourished,as did the still older Grammar schools and the public schools of the country. Of course, in these days great developments in the matter of education were taking place. The Government was soon going to assume its proper responsibility in the matter—a responsibility which he thought no other body in the country, religious or otherwise, was in a position to assume. It was the bounden duty of alltrue citizens to co-operate with the Government in order to render the efforts that were now being made,successful. He was quite sure that the Church which had so long co-operated with the Government in .times past, would continue to do so,and that the same might be said of the various Nonconformistbodies. At this crisis,a great re- sponsibility rested upon all the religious denominations to take care that no small differences interfered to thwart the great educational efforts that would have to be made. Of course, as regarded secular matters there could be no ' difficulty at all. He thought as regarded religious matters that no difficulty ought to arise. There was no reason in the world why the various religious bodies— at any rate the majority of them—should not come to an agreement with respect to the broad features of the religious education that ought to be given in the day schools. (Hear, hear.) If the new local authority which would have to be constituted undhr the Act were to ask the various ministers of religion to meet together and draw up a syllabus of religious instruction, he believed it could easily be done in a way that would be satis- factory to the great body of Christian people in War- rington. Of course, there might be some who would not see their way to fall in with a scheme of that kind, but to those he supposed the Conscience Clanse would apply, and some plan could be devised whereby they might have their own particular teaching given in their own way. He hoped the Town Council would try and meet their wishes in that respect. MR. JENKINS AND THE IMPERIAL FORCES. The toast of "The Imperial Forces" was proposed in suitable terms by Dr. BRAIDE and enthusiastically honoured. Mr. W. H. J. JMNKINS responded and expressed satis- faction that we as an Empire could at least hold our own. He had been very much struck during the past few days to see the breadth and strength of the British Empire as exemplified in the men who had so loyally .surrounded Earl Curzon at the splendid Durbar which had been held to proclaim the King, Emperor of India. In a recent speech at an educational conference lan McLaren said that boys should be trained and drilled in the art of self-protection and also in the principles of order and discipline so that they would be prepared to render assistance in times of danger and national neces- sity.He(Mr. Jenkins)the re-echoed sentiments expressed by lan McLaren. There could be no more beautiful thing I.in the world than that boys should be taught habits of cleanliness, order, and discipline,and he hoped no boy would be afraid to serve his country if necessityarose, either in the Navy,Army or reserve forces,and to conduct himself with credit and manliness. the thought. Paul maybe was right. He woul win yet! "Oh, ever so long," I answered vaguely--w uvpnrg." "Ton never told me," she said. "are you engaged to him, Rachel ? " "Silly child," I said, laughing; "what an ideal," "People don't saunter down lanes arm-in-arm if tiny are not engaged, and I can't think how you could know Mr. Ward. Mr. Densmore met Ithr abroad."

"11, was talking about you," I said, ignoring dim. latter part of her remark. .3 sweet, soft light came into her blue eyes, that Nias not the reflection of the firelight, but she turned her head aside to hide it from me.

"lie said you were 'sweetly frivolous.' "I added. "And, Irma, I really must go upstairs. Come' and have tea in the studio. Mr. Gerald is there." "Oh, no, I can't," she said. "I am going home; I don't want to meet Gerald." This was something else quite new. What had happened between her and Gerald? What time is it, Rachel ? " she added, linger- ing about me, and taking from my belt my little silver watch. "Why don't you buy yourself a gold watch and chain, Rachel, with all that money? Or a handsome bracelet watch would be nice. .

div.head: IRMA'S A\ DOFSG.
div.p: IRMA'S A\ DOFSG.
By ELLEN TIGHE HOPKINS, ' Author of "A Lost Lover," "Jack and JiL "When I was Twenty," "Will lie Win Her ? " "Reality,"

div.head: "I would as lid wear handcuffs as bracelets."
div.p: "I would as lid wear handcuffs as bracelets."
"Money is quite useless to you, Rachel. I should buy armfuls of lovely flowers and adorn the rooms."
"I don't like flowers in rooms."

"0 Rachel, and you pretend to love nature ! " "That isn't nature. I like flowers where nature put them, growing in the open air; not dying in vases. It is as bad as caged animals." "You are shocking, Rachel," she said, pretend- ing to shake me; "don't you love the ,darling old Zoo ? "

I "I would rather spend an afternoon in Portland Prison," I said, pinching her sweet, soft cheek; "the prisoners have, at least, sinned against the community, or it is presumed they have. The un- fortunate animals have no sins to expiate—so far as we know," I added doubtfully. "They may be expiating sins in a former life, who can say? But run, Irma; don't set me speculating. You caunot go home alone—it is quite dark." "Robert is waiting for me with the pony- carriage," she replied. "I galloped home alone from the hunt. Mr. Densmore will be scouring the country for me." "Are you staying at Mr. Densmore's ? " I asked. "How could you do such a thing, Irma? They will be dreadfully anxious about you." "I wanted them to be," she said defiantly. "Nonsense," I replied; "go and send a .telegrana at once, and let them know where you are," and I pushed her towards the window with a firm hand. "I shall go back, I think," she said; "there are some people to dinner to-night, and a little dance. Robert can drive me there instead of home." "And what reason will you give for remaining away like that ? " I asked. "Not any," she replied saucily ; "they .will say prayers over my safe return." She stepped lightly through the window as she spoke, and I watched until I saw her dimly in the dusk spring into the pony-car- riage. She was safe in old Robert's care, whether she went home or to the Densmores'. She must have seen me in the lane, and galloped home in a pet. Was she put out because she thought / was deceiving her? or did she care for Mr. Ward—otherwise Paul? And what would she say when she learnt the truth ? I almost felt angry that the happiness of such a man as Paul should lie in her wayward hands ; but, seeing that I could not resist her whimsical fascination my- self, could I wonder that my brother shared my weakness? I was still gazing absently •out into the dusky park, although the pony-carriage .had m long vanished from sight, when 'Thomas came into the library rather hurriedly. "Please, Miss Howard, Mr. Gerald is calling for you. My lady is not so well."

div.head: CHAPTER XI.
div.p: CHAPTER XI.

Ten days later I stood alone at the studio window, absently watching the rooks as they circled about the great bare branches of the trees with apparent aimlessness. Was there any method in their circling, any meaning in their noise? How less than nothing we know -of that which we can \ see—how hopeless to try and understand the !unseen!

Only when our eyes become blind shall we see— and how 'Long the time is! The sofa teside me was tenantless. The palette and brushes lay unsoiled. My friend and mistress had gone into the regions of which I desired so ardently to know more that my interest in erery- thing about me was, for the time being, almost blotted out. When would knowledge come to me? How long must it be before I stepped from dark- ness into the light?

Must I first le purified by suffering, as she had been? My coward spirit winced at that thought. The studio door opened with fussy gentleness. and Sir George entered on tiptoe, with a subdued air that did not sit easily upon him. His interest in all the ordinary detalls of everyday life was too keen for any sorrow to obliterate, and his vitality so strong that it was always a palpable effort to him to be quiet, or even to curb his vivacity. "Ah, I hoped I might. find you here, Miss Howard. t have a little business to settle, that I shall be glad to have out of hand." He walked across to my 'lady's bureau,, and my eyes followed him with some curiosity. I even experiei:ced a faint flutter of trepidation. Very faint it was ; it mattered so little what happened one way or the other: She was free from physical troubles, and I rated them very lightly: they are but milestones on the journey ; each time it is one more left behind, one step nearer the light that blinds our physical eyes. No further word had been uttered between us about the. diamonds or the puzzling miniature. Lady Isabella had been too ill for forty-eight. long hours for any of us to think of anything outside the chamber where she was giving her last strength to the lifting of the iron bar that lies across the Ivory Gate. Mr. Gerald and I eat many hours together through the weary night hours, watching the loosening .of the silver cord ; but. we neither of us thought of anything else; and the day after her funeral he started for India. He had exchanged into a regiment stationed at Boinlm,y, and left us all with but a brief and constrained farewell.
Sir George opened the bureau, and taking out the too well-known morocco cases, he brought them across and laid them down on a little table beside me.
"It was Lady Isabella's last wish that you should have these, Miss Howard," he said. • He took his hands from the cases, I fancied, with some reluctance, and 'slowly pushed them towards me.

I drew back sharply. "/"! Sir George; oh, please not! I should not know what to do with them." He looked up with a soniewhat sceptical smile, which faded as he realised my utter distress and consternation.

"It was her last urgent wish," he said. "She doubtleFs had good and sufficient reasons. I could not disregard such a bequest, Miss Howard." I was sobbing painfully; as I could not have sobbed for her death. . It was terribly hard to learn that after all I had failed to save her from the knowledge of her son's weakness. She must have known everything; she would never have left those diamonds to me otherwise; she knew how little I should value them. It was her strict sense of justice. Sir George was quite affected by my distress, though entirely misunderstanding the cause of it. "'To my most kind andl faithful friend.' Those were her words, Miss Howard," be said gently. • "I shall send them to Mr. Gerald, Sir George," I said hastily. - "I hardly think you can do that, Miss Howard," he replied, with more true dignity than I thought he could assume; and I was silent, realising how hopeless it was to try and set this matter right. We spin our webs ourselves; but only time can unweave them. I must wait in patience and in silence.

I sat there in the studio, with those two cases on the table before me, long after Sir George had left me, turning over in my mind various plans for getting rid of them. I was interrupted by the entrance of Thomas. "A gentleman, Miss Howard, in the library wishes to see you." "To see me!" I exclaimed. "Did he give his name, Thomas?" "Mr. Ward, miss." "Mr. Ward! What,is he like, Thomas?" "A tall, handsome gent, with a beard. I've seen him with Mr. Densmore." , My brother Pa-ill, of course! How stupid of me! I had forgotten his society name. I ran downstairs gladly, wondering as I went that a beard and different surroundings should so completely conceal Paul's identity. - - - . . .
_ Thomas, evidently, had not the faintest sus- picon on the subject. ft found Paul pacing restlessly about the library. His clear brown eyes shone with excitement.

"I have done it, Rachel," he said, seizing both my hands; "I have asked her, and she has accepted me. Said 'yes' so humbly and sweetly I could have knelt at her feet. I am madly happy, Rachel. She says she is not half good enough for me."

"She is quite right there, Paul. She is not; no one is. But have you told her ? " "Told her what?" "That you are Paul Howard," I answered. Some of the light left his eyes, and he looked at me anxiously. "Do you think it will make any difference, Rachel? If she loves me as she says, how can it? It is I whom she loves, not my name." "But you must tell her, Paul." "I suppose I must." he answered slowly, after a moment's hesitation. "But must I tell before we are married? " "You cannot be married under a false name," I said.

He did not answer, but paced thoughtfully to and fro, with an anxious look:that deepened as he walked. "And, Paul," I said gently, "would it be well to begin wedded life with a secret? If you do not lice telling her now, it would be worse after. Sh 6 could say unkind things with some truth then." "You are right. Rachel," he said, lifting his head proudly. "I will stand on my own merits, even if it cost me the dearest delight life holds." "That is my own brother," I replied; and I took his handsome head between my two hands ' and kissed him on both cheeks. "Well, I never! Rachel, lam surprised." The soft drawl was unmistakable. It came from the window. I turned quickly, and saw Irma in her riding-habit, her eyes and cheeks ablaze, her close-fitting waistcoat heaving with the tumult of her outraged feelings. She had stepped through the well-oiled French window unheard. For a moment we all stood transfixed ' - the position was so unexpected and so awkward. Then the ridiculous side of the matter struck me, and I laughed. Irma turned haughtily towards the open window, highly offended. We could not let her go like that. I ran after her. "Irma, you foolish child, come here. I will explain everything to you. I wa% only congratu- lating your future husband." In the Midst of her indignation Irma blushed a soft, rosy red, and shot a shy glance at her hand- some lover; but she was still very angry with me. "An extraordinary way of congratulating a gentleman," she said; "but you always Were an extraordinary woman, Rachel," and sweet Iron:, tried to look sarcastic. "We are an extraordinary family," I replied. "We none of us do quite what ordinary people do." "Indeed!" I was very near laughing again at Irma's lofty tone ; but I was really very anxious how she would take the truth, and my anxiety counteracted my disposition to laugh. How should we tell her? Patti cut the knot for me. "Irma, love," he said, going up to her, and bending his head over hers—and I noticed that the girl's whole being softened at his near approach —"lrma, love," Paul -repeated rather nervously, "will you forgive me for coming in disguise to win thy bride? " "In disguise ? " she said wonderingly. "Have you never recognised me, sweetheart?" he asked. "I have loved you all my life, Irma; since I was a little lad I have carried you in my heart of hearts." "You are Rachel's brother, Paul," she said in a whisper. Again, for a single long moment, we stood silent, we three, staring at one another. Paul stood as if turned to stone, but for his deep hard breathing, awaiting Irma's answer. Would she flout him, reproach him with haughty anger? Would she ridicule him? Who could foretell Irma's moods? I stood and watched • her heaving breast and flushing cheeks; not for worlds would I have said a word to her on one side or the other. This crowning moment of her life must be all her own. She did not prolong Paul's suffering unduly, or act with too great haste. She only glanced at Paul swiftly, as she said: "You are Rachel's brother, Paul," and then dropping her skirt and her whip she stood with her eyes bent on the floor, her colour coming and going nervously. Bet only for a minute or two. Euddenly lifting her head, she held out both hands to Paul, and exclaimed plaintively: "I have loved you longer than you have loved me, Paul; for I have loved you all my life." "My darling!" said Paul; and surely two words V, CIO never before made to express so much.

I had a letter from Gerald the next morning. A short, manly letter written just before sailing. "You have been my true friend, Mistress. Howard," he wrote, "and in the years to come I trust you will not repudiate that friendship_ There was perfect confidence between my mother and me at the last, and she gave me her full forgiveness. It was a madness."

. . . . . . . . . ;I think Irma has never regretted her decision. "He served seven years for me, as Jacob did for his wife, you know, Rachel," she said to ate inter on ; and this pretty conceit quiet reconciled her to ber democratic marriage. I let her keep it. -What use in trying to teach her the great spiritual lesson, of which Jacob and Rachel and the seven years are but an allegory?

Her time was not ripe. Some day I may tell you how she helped Paul to climb almost to top of the social ladder; how I eventually got rid of the diamonds with perfect satisfaction to everyone; and how Barton's Farm flourished. [Tim END.

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK.
THE LEYTON TRAGEDY.

One of most sensational murders of modern times has been revealed by the finding of three bodies, articulated and buried in sacks in the back garden of an unpretentious Essex villa; and never has our detective organisation shown to greater advantage. This gruesome find was in some way accidental, and the real feature of the case lies in the way in which the discoveries at 89, Church Road, Leyton, and 22, Wyndham Road, Camber- well, dovetail into each other. Edwards, as the prisoner is called, which name is supposed to be an alias, was arrested a few days back for a murderous assault on a grocer, called Garland, who has been critically ill as the result. In searching his house the police found many-suspicious things; and in the newly dug garden they discovered the dismemtered body of a man and a woman, to- gether with the corpse of a strangled baby. These have been identified as the remains of a grocer, called Darby, and his wife and child, who dis- appeared from Camberwell at the beginning of last month. By some clever deductive reasoning the police have fixed the exact time of the commission

ROAD, LEYTON,

div.head: IN "HZ GARDEN OF WHICH THE BODIES WERE FOUND,

cif the ctime between noon and 2 p.m. on the Ist of December, and their contention is that Edwards murdered all three single-handed, dis- posed of their bodies in Leyton, and transplanted their effects after them. If this theory be correct Edwards must be one of the most remarkable criminals of modern times, as seldom has such iron nerve or deliberate cold-bloodedness been exhibited in any murder. For boldness of conception and cool bluff, too, the story built up by the police is almost unparalleled. Edwards, it is alleged, en- deavoured to dispose of Garland in the same way; and it is his fortunate failure which has brought the other tragedy to light. The first floor at 22, Wyndham Road, Camberwell, is a veritable slaughterhouse; and the one point of difficulty is to understand how it was that suspicion of foul play was not aroused before at that end of the chain of circumstantill evidence. Edwards is now under remand, and an inquest on the Darbys is proceeding, and it is expected that many sensational facts will be brought to light.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF LORD CURRIE.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF LORD CURRIE.

Although Lord Currie's health has materially improved during the past few weeks, Sir Douglas Powell, under whose care he has been, thinks that he is not yet sufficiently restored to resume his duties as Ambassador at Rome without serious risk of r etarding his further recovery. He has, there- fore, placed his resignation in the hands of Lord -Lansdowne. as the extension of leave granted to him is about to expire. Lord Currie is a first baron being created such in 1899. He has been Am- bassador at Rome since 1898, and ha s performed his duties with exceptional ability. He may be said to have started life as a clerk on proba- tion in the Foreign Office till 1854, when he became junior clerk. In 1856 he was attached to the Legation at St. Petersburg. From 1857 to 1858 he was
LORD CURRIE,

precis writer to WHO, THROUGH ILL-HEALTH HAS the late Earl of RESIGNED THE POSITION OF AMBASSADOR AT ROME. Clarendon when he was Secretary for Foreign Affairs. In 1876 he was made secretary to Lord Salisbury's Special Embassy to Constantinople, and two years afterwards became Lord Salisbury's private secretary. In 1884 he was Assistant Secretary for Foreign Affairs, and five years afterwards was Permanent Under Secretary. He bed the position of Ambassador at Constan- tinople from 1893 to 1898. Lord Currie's successor be the Hon. Sir Francis Leveson-Bertie, K.C.8., Assistant Under Secretary to the Foreign Office.

div.head: END OF THE DURBAR.
div.p: THE END OF THE DURBAR.

The Durbar which concludes this week has turned out even more brilliantly than was antici- pated, and of all the Coronation ceremonies of King Edward VII. it has been without doubt the most gorgeous.. Delhi, with its long history of Oriental pageants has never seen a greater or more impressive sight than the parade and homage of the Indian potentates to the King. Emperor ; and tin those who are respon,ible for the " stage- management " of this affair the greatest honour is due, as it has gone off without the semblance of a hitch. All the great rajahs and chieftains were present in person—with ttie exception of one who was too ill to travel to Delhi—even down to the baby rajah on a baby elephant, who was one of the notable features of the procession; and all, including the Viceroy and the Duke of Connaught, were mounted on wonderfully trained elephants and rode in resplendent howdahs. These animals -numbered over Six hundred, and their salute, which was given like clockwork at the word of *command, was highly interesting and showed to what an extent these intelligent animals can be trained. Major Maxwell acted as herald and read his Majesty's proclamation to his Indian subjects in a very resonant voice; and Lord Curzon, after he and the Duke of Connaught had received the

div.head: SOUSA AND VIA BAND.
div.p: SOUSA AND VIA BAND.

John Philip Sows, whose concerts at the Queen's Hall during the past week have met with such success, has had an interesting career. His world famous hand is a thirty years' development, and may be said to date from the Peace Jubilee organised by Mr. P. S. Gilmore in Boston in 1872. In that monster musical festival the leading bands of Europe took part. Afterwards, at New York, Mr. Gilmore organised his famous band, in which he utilised all the most desirable characteristics of the foreign bands. For twenty years the Gilmore band enjoyed continuous prosperity and popularity; and " when in 1892 the baton fell from the life- less hand of Gil- more it was grasped by John Philip Sousa." He was at that time a famous bandmaster. Sousa began his connection with orchestras three and twenty years ago, for at the age of eleven he was playing the violin in public. Since he has had charge of his band he has played all through Ge r - many, Holland, JOHN PHIL Belgium, an d THE FAMOUS AMERICAN BAND- 'France, and last MASTER NOW IN ENGLAND. year through England and a portion of Scotland—not to forget Canada, from Vancouver to Prince Edward's Island. Speaking of the audiences of different countries Mr. Sousa says the human family is absolutely alike, and all the audiences before whom he has played have been the same so far as their appreciation and enthusiasm went. This famous conductor's mannerisms are in themselves sufficient to entice hundreds of ad- mirers. Certainly, these mannerisms, though they cannot have much effect on a band that knows the music by heart, are a study in histrionics. He apparently produces the most tremendous climax of noise by lifting his little finger with a gesture as if he were plucking a rose; at other times he genially pretends to lash his men to tremendous !eats.

div.head: MOROCCO SULTAN'S ASTUTE MOVE.
div.p: THE MOROCCO SULTAN'S ASTUTE MOVE.

It is to be hoped that at last affairs in Morocco Are approaching a peaceful termination as the result of the Sultan's astute move. The latter shows his energetic character and intelligence. He has caused to be brought from his place of im- prisonment at Mekinez his elder brother, Muley Mohammed, the very person whom the Pretender alleged that he wished to place on the throne. The Swltan made his formal entry into Fez, and was acclaimed by the populace, and after a public reconciliation with his brother, his Shoreefian Majesty, installed in his palace. announced that he appointed his brother Governor of the Province of Fez, thus disposing for the time being of the reports relative to the aspirations to the throne of Iluley Mohammed. As the result of this, the bribes in the Fez district have come in to swear
THE SULTAN OF MOROCCO AND THE TOWN
OF FEZ IN WHICH HE WAS THREATENED
WITH PROTRACTED BEIGE.

fidelity to the Sultan, declaring that Bu Hamara is an impostor, and that they would bar his way to Fez. Thus the immediate danger which has threatened Fez for many days was averted, and there is every reason to hope that this is the beginning of the end of the trouble. There is, however, the rumour that the Sultan still means war failing compliance with all his demands. Mohammed el Tores, Repre- sentative of the Sultan for Foreign Affairs; is reported to have said that the Pretender was acting on his own behalf, assisted by fanatics, and that his pretext for war was religious agitation.

div.head: EGYPTIAN HALL TO BE REBUILT.
div.p: THE EGYPTIAN HALL TO BE REBUILT.

The Egyptian Hall, which holds the distinction if being one of the oldest buildings in London used as a place of amusement, and which is certainly the home of more conjuring mysteries than any other erection in the world, is to be pulled down shortly. It was built in 1812 to be a Museum of Natural History. Almost at its opening it was used for the exhibition of the carriage in which Napoleon escaped from Waterloo. Since that time the build_ ing has been the home of some or other "ems-. tion." Al ter the Napoleon relic came' the Siamese twins, the double-sighted phenomenon, the Welsh dwarf, the centrifugal railway, the writing machine, Tom Thumb, talking machine, the largest horse in the world, the missing link, Annie Swan, the giantess, and Chang, the Chinese giant.
THE EGYPTIAN HALL, I.oNvo
WHICH IS SHORTLY TO I 1 IUIET.

The hall's first association with magic came with the arrival of Professor Pepper and bi.s glio•As. and Dr. Lynn, after which canto Maskelyne and (;)olc, with whom in this partietili..r branch of enter- tainment it has been asPociatcd CVOI7 snc. Mr. Maskelyne has just celebrated his :sixty- third birthday, and the thirtieth he has, :pent it the Egyptian Hall. It has been said that the ',mous illusiaist might long ago have made a rortun,l as the high priest of a new religion, or passed himself off as a spiritualist, or a clairvoyant, but, except as a showman, he has never made use of his tra- ordinary powers, and he has frequently in tae past thirty years been the means of exposing frauds. The reason the quaint old building is to he•de- molished is that Mr. MaskelynCs leae has expired and he has made arrangements for its being rebuilt on a larger scale, enabling the grei4 magician to produce even more stupendous wonders than heretofore. Mr. Maskelyne says he has for years been handicapped by want of space. There are only 3 ft. of room beneath the present stage and only 15 ft. at the back of the stage. In the new theatre he intends producing dramas in which magic takes a prominent place. A number of dramas might be named in which some form of ghostliness or spiritualism is iatroduced.' Take the ghost scenes in several of Shakespeare's plays, or the goblins in Rip Van Winkle. In the new hall Mr. Maskelyne • will show that plays necessitating the introduction of such mani- festations can be made far more realistic thaa anything that has yet been seen.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ANOTHER FOUR HOURS SITTING.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ANOTHER FOUR HOURS SITTING.

The ordinary meeting of the Warrington Town Coun- cil was held on Tuesday evening in the Town Hall, commencing at six o'clock. There was a large attend- ance of members and the important business on the agenda kept them fully Occupied until a few minutes to ten o'clock when the proceedings terminated abruptly through the sudden and serious illness of Councillor Baird. lie following were present :—The Mayor (Mr. J. C. Parr),the Deputy-Mayor (AldermanJ. Fairclough); Aldermen W. Bolton, Francomb, Hutchinson, Monks, Smethurst and Sutton; Councillors Baird, Barton, Bennett, Brophy, Burton, Craik, Davies, Dodds, James Evans, John Evans, Ellison, Forshaw Hulse„ Peacock, Pemberton, Pierpoint, J. Roberts, F. R. Roberts, W. Roberts, Rogers, Simpson, Tinnion, Upson, Wilkinson, with Messrs. J. L. Whittle (town clerk), S. Wilson (deputy-town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), J.Deas (water engineer), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), W. H. GrimAlale (electri- cal engineer), J. G. Gornall (medical officer). THE LATE MR. JOSEPH HARRISON J.P.

The MAYOR said is with deep regret I have to refer to the removal by death of one who has in times gone by,been an active, energetic, anduseful member of the Council, a man of conspicuous ability, persuasive eloquence and untiring energy, who was Mayor for three consecutive years, and had the honour of receiving the freedom of the borough, and notwithstanding his failing health and physical infirmity,maintained up to the last few years his connection with the many useful and beneficent institutions it was his pride and pleasure to assist with advice. With the businesslike experience he was able to give we shall all feel that we have lost a kind and a genial friend and a useful citizen. His Wor- ship moved a resolution to the effect that the Council received with deep regret the announcement of the death of Mr. Harrison, and regretted the great loss the borough had sustained by his death, and expressed the appreciation of the long and valuable publie services rendered by him, and that the Town Clerk be requested to convey to Mrs. Harrison and family the sincere sympathy of the Council with them in their sad bereave- ment."

The DEPUTY MAYOR seconded, and the motion was unanimously agreed to. • A HAPPY NEW YEAR" FROM THE MAYOR. His WORSHIP then said: "At this our first Counoil meeting of 1903,1 hope I may beallowed to wish youall from my heart "a veryhappy new year." May it also be a happy and a prosperous year for our town of Warring- ton and its many inhabitants, and may God's blessing be with us that our counsels maybe guided for the good of those for whom we are called upon to legislate. It is our earnest hope and intention (for I feel sure that I may speak for the whole Council as I do for myself) to transact the business .that conies before us in a straightforward, businesslike, honest and honourable manner, to practice all reasonable economy, compatible with efficiency, and a due regard to the exigencies of the times and their many and varied requirements. (Hear, hear.) He also referred to the consideration and support he had received during the previous year and again hoped "that our deliberations will still be charao- terised by the dignity, the good order, and public spirit which so far have been accorded to my presidency, and which Iso thankfully appreciate." (Applause.)
PROPERTY-OWNERS AND THE COST OF STREET MAKING.
COMPULSORY MEASURES BY THE FINANCE COMMITTEE. "A HIGH-HANDED PROCEEDING."

At a meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee, held on the Ist December, it was resolved that Alder- man Shaw Greenand Alderman Fairclough be appointed members of the Property Purchasing Committee. The Borough treasurer submitted a list of over-due accounts for street making, when it was resolved, that the Town Clerk take proceedings for the recovery of the same, and that in such cases as he may deem it advisable Mr. Joseph Smith be appointed receiver on behalf of the Corporation; and that the balance of the purchase money of the Feathers Hotel due from the Liverpool and District Public House Trust Company, Limited, be allowed to remain on mortgage at interest of four per cent. per annum; while at a meeting on the 15th December, it was resolved, that in the opinion of this committee, the premises at Market-gate, now occupied by the Union Bank of Manchester, Limited, and others, and the premises occupied by Briggs and Company and others, should be pulled down for the improvement of Market-gate. The DEPUTY-MAYOR proposed the adoption of the minutes. Alderman MONKS seconded.

Councillor FORSHAW said he thought it was rather high-handed proceeding to appoint a receiver of property because some of the accornts for street-making had no been paid. He thought if a little further time were given to the property owners, they would pay their accounts. He moved that%tho resolution be referred back to the committee. Couneillor JAMES EVAN'S seconded,and said the reso- lution struck him as being a very unusual proceeding Knowing that there was a considerable feeling upon this question of street-making, had it not been that there were several notices of motion down, and that the meet- ing would probably ben lengthy one, he would have put in a notice of motion concerning this particular resolu- tion and street-making generally. He would do so for the next meeting. There was considerable dissatis- faction among those who had to pay for street-making rather extensively, and a large number of them were objecting. Some of the persons who were having to pay. had emphatically told him that they were not receiving value for the money they were asked to pay. The MAYOR said he was reminded that this point was not under discussion._
Councillor JAMES EVANS said he would reserve his further observations until he brought forward his notice of motion. _ _
Councillor BURTON supported the amendment; but not for the reasons given by Councillor Evans. He said the streets were not properly paved. There was a grave doubt about it.

He thought the three years' time allowed was altogether too little. It should.be live or six.

He contended that the time was too short, and said that in many of the out districts ten years was given. He thought this matter ought not to be left to the discretion of one official. It ought to be in the ,discretion of the com- mittee. _

It was a high-handed proceeding coming from any committee. Unless he had further informa- tion he should vote against the committee. Alderman MONKS said there was no desire whatever !on the part of the Committee. to deal with these in. dividuals in any hard way. It was well known that the I money for the making of these streets was due on de- maud, but the Council had dez.nded that the owners could sign an agreement for the tinie,duriug which the money was to be paid to be extended for three years. But some of these people could well afford to pay and ! would not. Some of the amounts due were as much as three years behind. Nothing had been paid by the owners since the agreement was signed, not a half-penny either of principal or interest. It was a. deliberate at- tempt on the part of these people to defy the Com- mittee. (Hear, hear). div.head: Smallpox at Widnes.
div.p: Smallpox at Widnes.

A further case of smallpox has been discovered at Widnes. On Saturday, James Hodgkinson, a Widnes maQ., who had been lodging at a common lodging- house at No. 3, Victoria-street, Widnes, was admitted to the workhouse infirmary suffering from fever. The case has since developed int) one of small-pox. The lodging-house, and 18 to 20 occupants have been quarantined.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

HILL CLIFFE CLUB DIVIDE.—The annual meeting of the Hill Cliffe Baptist school club was held the other evening in the schoolroom, when there was a good at- tendance of teachers and members. The accounts for the year were presented. Sick pay had been made to six scholars, and a dividend of nearly four shillings each was declared, which was then distributed, nearly £2O ; being thus divided. Thanks were accorded to the President, the Rev J. S. Hughes; E. England, treasurer; and G. Moss, secretary. A number of new rules were adopted, and officers appointed for the year.

A. PAINTER'S DEATir:—Mr. R. Dobson, coroner, Con— ducted an inquest at Red Lion Inn, Stockton Heath, on Monday,touching the death of a painter named Walter Burge, 3, Jockey-street, Warrington, which took place on January Ist, at Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath. The deceased, who lived with his sister in Jockey-street, had beefi unwell for 18 months. Dr.Cartis- attended him from the end of 1901 to April last. when he recommended him to go to the Manchester Hospital for Consumption and Diseases of the. Throat. He stayed at . the hospital for a considerable time, but ultimately the case proved to be hopeless, and he was recommended to "get into the fresh air." In consequence deceased was staying at Stockton Heath on the 20th orDecember. He saw an advertisement in a newspaper and applied to the advertiser for certain remedies. He received a bottle of syrup. a bottle of oil, packet of herbs, a typewritten letter of directions, anda book, entitled" Hope for the Hopeless," for which he paid three guineas. While stav- ing at Stockton Heath, the deceased seemed better. bilt became worse on Christmf.is morning. He seemedafter- wards to be at a standstill until he died- suddenly on January lst.—Dr. Curtis said he was of the opinion'that the articles sent as advertised were absolutely harmless. The cause of death wasconsumption of the throat. A verdict was returned to this effect.

AN almost universal satis JOHN BULL'S fastion has been oceas- BURDENS. sioned by the agreement

at which the Irish Land Conference found it possible to arrive. The settle- ment of the laud question would be equivalent to the extinction of the chief of Ireland's grievances. It would be worth almost any price that could be paid for it. And yet the cost would necessarily be so heavy that those by whom it had to be paid might well be excused if they pulled somawhat of a wry face. When a body of representative Irish landlords finds itself in agreement on a land-pur- chase question with men like Mr. JOHN REDM )ND and Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, the scheme whch they are disposed to recommend demands some careful scrutiny from tile British taxpayer, who must find the funds for whatever plan of settlement may be finally adopted by the legislature. Neith m- the Irish landlords nor the Irish patriots have ever 'been dispoced to spare the pockets of the pre- dominant partner. When they come into agree- ment, therefore, it Is natural to supposo that it is on terms mutually advantageous, or, as they would no doubt themselves prefer to put it, on terms specially advantageous to Ireland. And this, in fact, is what has occurred. It is proposed to sub- stitute an occupying proprietary for the existing system of dual ownership; but the price to be paid by the owners is not to be based on a valua- tion, but on income. This means, of course,that the rack-renting landowner would have to be bought out, not on the actual value of his pro- perty, but on the basis of his rack-rents. The most extreme of Irish landlords—the DUKE of ABERCORN or Loan BARRYMORE, let us say—might well be satisfied to fall in with an arrangement like this. It is the State, of course, that is to provide the money for the transaction. The purchase price is to consist 'either of an assurance by the State of such income, or the payment of a capital sum produc- ing such income at 3 per cent, or at 3+ per cent if guaranteed by the State." So much for the landowners. Then as to the tenants. The amount of purchase-money payable is to he extended over a long series of years, and to be at such a rate as will at once secure a reduction of not less than 15 or more than '25 per cent on what are called second- tern rents. For such a scheme as this Mr. T. W. Russell is willing that the country should make great sacrifices. He is willing, that is to say, to buy out the landlords at thirty-three years' pur- chase of their incomes, though he has previously declared that twenty-three years' purchase are the terms to which they are really entitled. We repeat that for the settlement of the Irish land grievance, hardly any price won! I be exces- sive but can we afford to go on contemplating schemes like this, as ii every room at the Treasury

were a sort of cave of Monte Christ° ? We have purchased pease in South Africa; we have attempted to purchase the goodwill of the sugar- planters in South Africa; we are plunging from big wars into little wars; we are spending millions in making a foolish railway in Uganda. In all possible directions we are behaving as if the pocket of the British taxpayer were an inexhausti- ble mine of wealth. Meantime, the normal expendi- ture of the country may be set down at £150,000,000 —an increase of £80,000,000 in thirty years. A mast addition has been made to the National Debt, the Sinking Fund has been suspended, and the in- ceree-tax stands at is. 3d., so that it is practically impoksible to put a further strain on. that easy and -tempting means of raising revenue. We have not yet found out how much it is possible for the coun- try to bear in prosperous times. Successive Tory Chancellors of the Exchequer, constantly raising the national eipenditurn above what may be cslled the flood-marks of previous years, have always obtained what they have asked for without trouble, and without apparent strain on the public patience; but we have for some years .pastbeen living to a large extent on the national capital, and now that we are ceasing to do this the tide of our industrial prosperity has turned. We may find before long that even our existing burdens are such as we must stagger under. The .present GoOernment has dealt with our finances as if there could be no possible recurrence of bad trade, and therefore of diminished incomes; but here, just when we have reached our highest level •of exeenditure, a period of bad trade sets in, and there is a loud cry for help from the industral poor. It may turn out, therefore, that the Irish flandlords have been too long in coming to terms With those whom they have persistently regarded W; their enemies. Judge O'CONNOR MORRIS,K keen --student cf the land question, has been telling an Irish grand jury that there will be no satisfactory Land Bill during the next session of Parliament; and, considering what is our financial position,and 'What are the terms that alone content the Irish 'landlords, we are disposed to think that he has formed a correct judgment of the situation.

ONE of our metropoli. THE CHURCHES AND tan contemporaries is THE PEOPLE. taking what it calls a religious census of 'London. It is really enumerating those who who attend church, chapel, or mission-hall with .more or less regularity. The assumption is that the counting will be done on an average day, and that on the particular Sunday chosen by the enu- merators the attendance will be pretty much what it is on most other Sundays. There has always been a strong objection to the taking of a relig- ious census by the State. The reason is in general we believe, vaguely understood ; yet it is a good, commonplace reason, sound enough to have de- terred successive Governments frown putting a " religion" column in the census paper. Based, as it would be, on the assumption that all those who do not belong to other religious sects are ''ambers of the Church of England, it must necessarily be unfair to the smaller bodies of denominationalists. Those who never entered a Place of worship would be put down to the credit .of the Established Church. The late Professor iirrxr.BY found himself described on one occasion as a member of the Church ot England; and when he Protested, and asked for an explanation, it was Proved to him that the description was legally exact. Obviously, a Church which sweeps men into its net in this daring fashion would in a religious census obtain a predomivauce to which on other grounds it was not entitled. There was an informal religious census, which was published as a Blue-nook, some time between the forties and the fifties ; but it settled nothing, the number of persons belonging to the various Churches being estimated rather than actually ascertained. We have, in consequence,no certain knowledge of what is the relativeposition of the various Churches in the country. We do not know whether Churth people or Nonconformists are in the majority. It would probably be found, if a census b Lsed on attendanca were taken throughout the whole Country, that the Established Church is the 'Church of a minority. This cannot be said in regard to London, however, so far, at least, as the voluntary enumeration of our contemporary has gone. Of the Londoners who attend places of Worship, slightly more than half prefer the services •of the Church of England. This result may be altered when the full totals are known. it is mainly in the wealthier districts of London that the enumeration has been carrieci out up to this time. Where the takers of the religious census have gone into poor neighbourhoods they have generally found the Church of England in a minority.

In Battersea, for example, those who attended 'Church of England services on a particular Sunday numbered only 11,665, against a total attendance of 26,992. The St. Pancras district presents us with similar results. Oat of the total attendance of 39,850, only 17,275 attended the churches of the Establishmentit would appeac,therefore,as might, indeed, have been surmise 1, that the " national" Church has a much less firm hold of the poor and of the middle-slas3 than of the classes higher up in the social scale. "We are here tilue of n-4 Nonconformists," said the EARL of ROSEBERY n the House of Lords the other week. That is true of the higher circles almost generally. Their religion is the religion of the State. But for definite conclusions on points like these the religion .‘"neus of London is not slfficiently advanced. ‘lThat is most striking about the figures at present, iS tile extent to which they reveal, the indifference of the great bulk of the people to religiuns worship. UP to the present the church attendance of a PePulation amounting to 1,340,699 has been enumerated. Out of this number only 266,514 went to places of worship of any kind on the days chosen for the enumeration. Roughly, this is one in five, or less. It is not to be crbncluded, ho AY - ever, that all those who failed to attend a religious service on a particular Sunday are habitual absentees. Many of them, no doubt, go to places of worship occasionally ; some were unavoidably absent; and still more,no doubt, were having what they might call their " &Inlay off." Whatever deductions in,- Y be made, however, the 'figures are a most remarkable revelation of the Teebleness of the gram) of the various Church( s over the population of London. Those who attend places of worship are, numerically, like a floating island in a sea of indifferentism. And in this res- pect, it seems, things are going from bad to worse. The attendance, in proportion to population, does not tend to increase, but diminish. Why should this be The question is one which all the Churches ought to put to themselves in a spirit of Tight down earnestness.

New bye-laws drawn up by the Cheshire County Council for the "good rule and government " of the county have just come into force, and particu- lars will be found among the public notices On our first page. The interests of cyclists seem to hive had special consideration, and perhaps thia is only fair seEing what a cyclists' pAradise Ches- hire is. They probably form a large majority of the road-users in the County, and it is pleasing to note that the already well-kept highways of the "C.C.C." ark to be still further protezted. Those careless people who leave broken glass lying about and those who neglect to remove the hedgecut- tinge, will, in future, all be liable to a penalty of 403. Another sensible provision ensures orderly behaviour on the Sabbath. The thoughl.-2ss individuals who go careering about the County in waggonettes and the like to the accompaniment of horn and trumpet solos, noisy songs, etc., will in future be liable to a similar penalty if the annoyance is occasioned on Sunday. Residents, not only of Cheshire itself, but of the neighbouring counties, will welcome these new regulations and breathe a blessing on the County Council for its wise forethought and kindly consideration.

Again the returns of British commerce with the Colonies and foreign countries offer a surprise to the pessimists. We have been told until the news has become a mere commonplace that trade is in a bad way. Yet the Board of Trade report, shows an increase of imports though a slight decrease of exports for the month of December. while the completed figures for 1902 place both incoming and outgoing trade in advance of that of the previous year. Even with regard to the exports for December, a little examination puts a different complexion on the decrease, wiaich then appears to be mainly due to the drop in exported shipping, an item on which a month's figures may give • a very misleading impression and which really requires averaging over a much longer period. It must be admitted that of the different heads under which exports are divided this is the one which gives the greatest cause for anxiety. The exported shipping for the year fell off by a very wide margin from that of 1901, and there are evidences, too serious to be disregarded, of depression in the trade, such as the notice of d. crease of wages to the ship-building employees on the Clyde. Yet when it is seen that notwith- standing this decrease a large majority of the whole worid's shipping was built in British ports, it can- not be contended that things are very had. S far as the figures go they shew a year of i;rosper- ity, a year of advance upon that preceding it, and even, though by a very slight margin, upon 1900

THE LICENSING SESSION:, Sir Richard Brookeand Mr. %V. Timmins,sittingat the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, fixed February 9th as the date of the annual licensing sessions. WESTON POINT BIBLE CLASS.

In connection with the Weston Point Wesleyan Adult Bible Class the second annual social and prize distribu- tion was held on Wednesday evening. Mr. Rossenburg presided, Mrs. Baker distributing the prizes to over 50 persons. An interesting concert was afterwards held,at which Messrs. R. Morris, G. Johnson, Mr. end Mrs. Leathwood, and the Camden quartette party contributed items.

div.head: SUCCESS OF LOCAL CHOIR BOYS.
div.p: SUCCESS OF LOCAL CHOIR BOYS.

The following boys have gained special prizes for regular attendance at the Parish Church :—Aithut Goldsmith. Arthur Rathbone, James Scott, John Wooley, Charles Wilkinson. Arthur Rathbone gains a special prize for the third year in succession. It is interesting to know that these boys have never missed a single prac- tice or Sunday service, never losing a mark for bad con- duct or inattention. CRUELTY CASE AT WIDNES.

. - At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. E. J. Mu.spratt and Mr. Thomas, Owen and John M'Connell, hay and straw dealers, Oreillell-street, were ordered to pay 10s. and costs or fourteen days in default for cruelly illtreating and starving two ponies. The evidence of the inspector of the Society for the Pre- vention of Cruelty to Animals and a police-constable showed that the animals were in a fearful condition from being insuffleintly fed.
THE MERSEY MISSION ENTERTAINS 200 CHILDREN.

On Friday evening about 200 Sunday school scholars connected with the Mersey Mission to Seamen were entertained to ton at the Seamen's Institute. .The principal feature of the entertainment was a splendid Punch and Judy show given by Professor Fraser-Jones. Needless to stty this well-knownartist kept his audience in screams of laughter for fully half an hour during which time he introduced the art of shadowgraphy per- forming some really wonderful feats. The distribution of prizes from the Christmas tree-was performed by Mr. Bateson. On the motion of Mr. Shaw (the missionary), seconded by Mr. E. Good, ahe trty vote of thanks was passed to the friends who had subscribed the funds for the tea and prizes. A similar vote was accoriei to Mr. Bateson for present;ng the prizes. THE NEW LICF.NSING ACT.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Sir Richard Brooke and Mr.'W. Timmins, George Herbert, Andrews applied for temporary authority to sell until the next transfer day at the Elephant and Castle Inn, Halton. Edward Alexander ;Jones applied for temporary authority to sell at the Bird in Hand Inn,- 11,t1ton-ro:od, lately occupied by Mr. Andrews.—Mr. F. Johnson (magistrates' clerk) said the new Licensing Act required seven days' notice to be given of these applications.— The Chairman said it was a question whether the police had any objection.—Superintendent Ennion said he had no objection.—The applications were accordingly granted.—The Magistrates' Clerk informed the appli- cants that under the new Act they would be required to produce their tenancy agreements at the transfer sessions.

div.head: TRAMP SENT TO GOAL.
div.p: A TRAMP SENT TO GOAL.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday moinhy, before Messrs. F. J. Norman (in the chair), and 2. Imison, a tramp named Fred Thompson was summoned for refusing to do his alloted task and tearing his clothes.—Mr. Cunnah, master at Dutton Workhouse, said that on Tuesday night the prisoner tore up his clothes and refused to pick the four pqunds of oakum given him to do. He said he wanted to go to gaol. He refused to be made presentable to come to court, and consequently appeared only in trousers, shirt awl bare feet. Prisoner said in reply to the charge that on Mim- day night, when he asked for admittance, he was kept outside inthe rain for over an hour, and that the master refused to have his clothes stored which were verminous. —Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month.

A GHASTLY FIND AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn Police Station on Friday morning, Mr. R. Dobson, district coroner, inquired into the cir- cnmstances'attending the death of Sylvanns Walker, a salt lofter, whose body was • found in a lock of the Bridgewater Canal on Wednesday, Sarah Walker, wife of Enoch Walker, 55,Percivars-lane, Runcorn, said deceased was-her son. She last saw him alive at a quarter to eight on the night of December 6th. He had complained of pains in his head for two days. What the complaint was exactly she could not state, but he had had a drop of drink. He. how‘ever,had none except at the end of the week. He followed his work up to Friday night. She reported his disappear- ance to the police.—By a juror: The workmen told her that he was strange in his manner on the Thursday night. The police spoke to the finding of .the body in one of the locks, while a woman named Annie Smith, 47 Percival-lane, saw the deceased walking by the canal IT the night of his disappearance.—.-k verdict of Pound Drowned" was. returned.

div.head: T e Examiner, Friday, January 9, 1903.
div.p: T e Examiner, Friday, January 9, 1903.

SONS OF TEMPERANCE.—INTERESTING PRESENTATION. On Saturday evening a meeting of the Sons of Tem- perance Order was held in the Greenway-road school- room, Runcorn. Mr. Thomas Clarke presided. Three new members were initiated and several proposed for membership.—Mr. Bisbrown said that since their last meeting the temperance cause had sustained a very great loss by the death of the Archbishop of Canterbury who, as everyone knew, was a teetotaller and a tower of strength to the movement. He was intensely interested in temperance work, and for more than thirty years in the pulpit and on the platform had furthered the cause. The following officers also spoke in warm appreciation of the late Primate: Mr. Thomas J. Holt, Mr. Thomas Heesom,Mr. Thomas Cooke and the Chairman.—Mr. Thomas Cooke then installed the newly-elected officers. —Mr. G. Powell, the new president, thanked the mem- bers for having elected him to the chair. He then.in the name of the division, presented Mr. Clarke with a beauti- ful emblem framed in oak bearing the inscription: "Lifeboat Crew Division, No. 195 : Resolved that the best thanks of the sub-division be and are hereby tendered to Bro. Thomas Clarke for his valuable services as Worthy Patriarch for two terms. George Powell, W.P., John Cooke, F.S., January 3, 1903."—The follow- ing officers heartily supported the resolution and spoke of thefible manner in which Mr. Clarke had conducted the business of the Order: Messrs. Thomas Heesom, W. Bisbrown,Thomas J. bit, Thomas Cooke, Edward Key, jun.. Thomas R. Whyte; and William Hazlehurst, of Weston.—Mr. Clarke replied, and thanked the members for their past kindness to him and said he was proud to be associated with them.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT].

Runcorn people will be pleased to hear that the two sons of our respected and public spirited townsman, Mr. Francis Wiswall C.E., ex-chairman of the Urban Council have just achieved signal successes in the professional careers they have chosen for themselves. Mr. Walter H. Wiswall the eldest son and his father's chief assistant as engineer to the Bridgewater Canal, has just passed the entrance examination, qualifying him for elec- tion as an associate of the Institute of Civil Engineers. The examination was held in London and occupied three days, the subject covering a wide range in science and engineering. We compliment Mr. Wis- wall upon his success, wh ch is a natural result of his attainments at Liverpool University College to Runcorn Technical Institute. He is the possessor of first class Science and Art Department's certificates, both for the elementary and advanced stages, in each of the follow- ing subjects :—Steam, naval architecture, machine con- struction and drawing, and magnetism and electricity. For advanced applied mechanics he holds a first class certificate; also mathematics,stages I. and 111. 2nd class, stage 11., Ist class. He has further passed Ist class, the Liverpool University College engineering examination. In addition to those enumerated, Mr. Wiswall holds four. teen other science certificates. This is a record of which he has every reason to be proud

His brother Mr. John W. Wiswall. also employed in his father's office, has also obtained well merited dis- tinction. He has been elected a graduate of the Institute of Mechanical Engineers doubtless a step towards further honours. His scholastic records in science is highly creditable. At present he is the holder of a County Council scholarship at Runcorn Technical in- stitute Evening School and is the possessor of the fol- lowing Science and Art Departments Certificates : Machine construction and drawing Ist E. and Ist A., applied mechanics Ist E, 2nd A ; naval architecture Ist E, 2nd A; mathematics, Ist B; practical mathematics Ist A; physics, magnetism and electricity, and theore- tical mechanics Ist B. Mr. John Wiswail has further secured aflrst class certificate for mechanical engineer- ing in connection with the Londno Institute.

The exhibition of students' work and tradesmen's exhibits was in every respect, save, perhaps, the attend- ance of the public, a marked success. No one would have thought it possible for a town like Runcorn to have produced such a varied and interesting collection. Those who visited the exhibition must, necessarily, have had their intellect strengthened and their experience broadened. The promoters have every reason to con- gratulate themselves upon the result achieved. There can be no questioning the fact that the tradesmen of Runcorn, judging by the evidence submitted at the Institute, are not one whit behind their confreres of the larger towns for technical ability and quality of work- manship; while among the students are some who evidently will, sooner orlater,. make for themselves by no means an unknown name in their several depart- ments. It will be a great mistake, from an educational point of view, if the exhibition does not become an annual institution.

So the Board of Trade have actually refused to allow he Electric Lighting Order, .obtained at such a cost and which has simply remained in the Council's safe' to be in force longer than a few months. The Council, in the meantime, will have to do something with it or else the Order will quickly be worth bqt the value of the paper it is written on. Mr. Handley evidently th7nks the town will be able to derive certain advantages from the Electric Company, which is seeking to erect an electric lighting si:ntion near Rocksavage, that the town could not have gained if they had not ' obtained the Order. This is certainly taking an optimistic view of a very del:cate situation; .but whether it is a justifia;3le atti- tude remains to be seen. it must not be forgotten that a drowning wan will clutch at a straw; similarly it ap- pears that the Council is ready to avail itself of any little chance puff of wind which will enable them to steer, with dignity, out of a very awkward predica- ment.

The New Licensing Act has not yet been officially put into force at Runcorn. It may be, interesting to chronicle a fact given on substantial authoray. Two local working men. who had been in the habit of spend- ing their time pretty frequently in the bar-parlour of a well-known Boniface, have actually "signed teetotal" lest they should unwittingly come under clauses of the new Act—which, by the way seem to be regarded with a certain amoant of terror by a ceKain section. It is not to be expected thai, the men will keep thei*self im- posed pledge, but at all events the spirit seems willing though the flesh may prove, in the long rim, weak. After this we shall have to reConsiderour nat;onal axiom that "you cannot make a man sober by an Act of Parlia- ment.'

THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. THE . SMALL-PDX VISITANT.

The Medical Officer reported that the number of deaths during the last month was sixteen. Fifty-four births were registered. In the corresponding month of last year Clore were forty-two births and thirty-fonr deaths. The report proceeded: It will be within the knowledge (4 the authority from what has already appeared in the Press that a tramping quarryman found his way into one of the lodging houses of the town. He left the town on Tuesday week and visited a neighbour- ing town where he was found to be suffering from small-pox. The bed on which he slept in the lodging- house has been destroyed, the bed clothing disinfected, the room thoroughly washed and fumigated and several of the inmates have been • revaccinated. The lodging- houses of the town are at present under constnet sur• veillence and supervision and there has been so far no fresh development. The Chairman said it was satisfactory to know that the officials had taken such prompt m-easures to prevent the spread of the small-pox epidemic. Mr. Dean said.the town Owed a debt of.gratitr.de to those who hnd acted so pro:aptly in preventing the spread of such a loathsome disease.

div.head: TO PREVENT DIPIITHERTA.
div.p: TO PREVENT DIPIITHERTA.

The Health Committee recommended that this Coun- cil provide, free of cost. diphtheril anti-tox;n, to any person unable to pay, through the patient's medical pract'tioner. Dr. Dean said it was a new departure but it was in the right direction. If the providing of anti-toxin free, would prevent the spread of diphtheria the result would be worth the expend; ture. Mr. Jones seconded and the minutes were approved.
FIREMEN'S DANGERS AND COMPENSATION.

The Markets and Cemetery Committee recommended that the report prepared by the Secretary as to the exacution of the Canal Boats Acts, be approved and adopted. Mn. Gatley proposed the'adoption of the minutes. remarking that the committee regretted the increase of children on the boats. The committee were especially gratified at the prompt action of the fire brigade at the recent fire in a central part of the town in preventing it from spreading. They were especially sorry to learn that the Superintendent had met with. an accident at the fire and trusted he had recovered. - -

FOOTILILL.

I After the magnificent display Earlestown made against St. Helens Rees, it was a sore disappointment to their supporters to witness the wretched performance against St.Helens town on New Year's day. When playing the Recs. the forwards could do nothing wrong. but against the town, the reverse was the case and they could do • nothing right, in fact a lot of school boys could have done almost as w911.-Iney certainly deserved the thrash- ing of 3 goals to I whch they received.

The following day they had Bacup as visitors in the Rawcliffe Charity Cup Competition, but although the play was of a med:ocre character, they managed to beat Bacup by 2 goals to 1, and this is the team a few weekc agoEarlestown defeated by about 8 goals. Football is certainly a mysterious game, and the results cannot be foretold.

-- I On Saturday Earlestown had a long journey to Barrow to play a league fixture and here again the uncertainties of the game were exemplified. Several of the Elides- • town players did not turn up, and a scratch team had to be got together. Despite this however, they gave Barrow • a good game but in the end they had to suffer defeat by , 2 goals to 1.
! They are at home to-morrow, Saturday, to Working- ton, when it is hoped they will be able to secure a much ; needed coupla of points.
