Au " open session " was conducted by Mr. Stout at the Spiritualist Hall on Sunday afternoon, and was well attended. After the usual opening exercises, silver and golden chain recitations and musical read- ing, marching and calisthenics, the prizes for regu- larity of attendance and good conduct, 21 in number, were distributed in. a very graceful manner by Miss Furness, who has just concluded two years term of office as conductress. 'Mr. Joseph. Foster officiated as musical director, Mr. Foster, sen., as conductor of the marching, and Mr. IV, Massey, the new con- ductor, led the calisthenics. The whole pro- ceedings were of a very pleasing character.— In the evening Miss Jones, of Liverpool, delivered a thoroughly • spiritual address on " Hallowed be Thy Name, in earth as it is in heaven," followed by a little clairvoyance. On Mondny evening, in the absence of the appointed medium through. illness, a .public circle was held, several local mediums render- ing efficient service.—On Tueday evening Mr. Ernest Marklew, formerly a frequent visitor to this society, delivered a telling address on " The best feature in Spiritualism," in which he stated his conviction that of all its valuable features the best was the effect of its moral teaching in regulating conduct in this life, which was the best means of attaining happiness in this world and in the next.

div.head: Golden Wedding of Sergeant and Mrs. W. Bodle.
div.p: Golden Wedding of Sergeant and Mrs. W. Bodle.

l'his event was celebrated on Saturday last at Toft's Assembly Room., Bridge-street. About 60 guests sat down to a sumptuous tea which was in the capable 'hands of Messrs. Toft and Son. The bride- groom who has seen service in the Crimea,. had a good reception, and after the inner man had been attended to Mr. W. Fletcher proposed the health of the bride and bridegroom, and spoke about the ser- vices rendered by the Sergeant to his father, ,Mr. Bodle having been in Mr. Fletcher's employ for over a quarter of a century and had always done • all he could for the upbuilding of the trade and had been the first mini in his employ. Mr. W. Fletcher was unable , to attend owing to ill-health. Mr. Weaver secinded the proposition. Mr. Walton,of Manchester supported ' the same. Miss Bodle then sang effectively "Darby and Joan." The Rev. W. Carnson proposed the health of the ladies. Quartermaster-Sergeant Jack- son Made a humorous seconder, and Miss Dutton, 'of Moore responded on behalf of the ladies. " Our Guests " was proposed by Mr. W. Bodle, jun: The remainder of the evening .vas spent in listening to the strains of music from the gramaphone of Mr. T. Bodle, solgs and recitations by Miss Bodle, Mr Walton and; Mr. Garthual. Mr. George Weaver, jnn.;-; occompanied.• Amongst the guests were Mr. W. and I Miss Fletcher (Grappenhall), Mr. and Mrs Walton (Manchester), Mrs. • Pennv (Ramsgate), Quartermaster- Sergeant J. Jackson (Shorneliffe), Mr. and Mrs. G. We ver, Mr. and Mrs. Barlow, Mr. and Mrs. J Weaver, Mr. and Mrs. Bate, Mr. Dunn, Mrs. Hedgcock, and members of the family.--A number or handsome ! presents were received.

DEATH OF MRs. J. SMITH, NEWTON. Mrs. Smith, relict of the late Mr. James Smith, of Brookside, Newton, passed away early on Wednesday morning at the age of 68 years. She has been some- what of an invalid for about 20 years, but it was only a few months ago that she was taken seriously ill. She went to Colwyn Bay in September, and whilst there was taken ill, and has not since been out of bed except to be removed home. She has been assiduously attended by Dr. Harold Watkins, but since Christmas there has been little hope of recovery, the immediate cause of death being syncope. She leaves four sons and three daughters, all of whom, with the exception of the younger son, are married. A short service will be held in Newton Church at 11 o'clock on Saturday morning, and the funeral will take place at Ince Cemetery. UNHAPPY MARRIED LIFE AT GOLBORNE.

Rosannah O'Neill, of Golborne, char-ge-cfl;i—hUsband, Patrick O'Neill, at Newton Petty Sessions,on Thursday, with persistent cruelty. Mr. W. B. Johnson, of Wigan, defended. Mrs. 0' Neill.stated in her evidence that a mutual sepandion was made, andlafterwards she wrote for him to come back. She alleged that when he did come back he ran her round the table and tried to put her on the fire. He dragged a shawl from her head, and the pin with which it was fastened stuck in her neck She had since been in the Wigan Infirmary.—The defence was a denial of the cruelty. He had been good to her and since he had been back had bought a piano and sew- ing machine, and allowed her 28s. to 30s. a week. Con- stable Wild spoke to being called to the house in May last, and seeing defendant bleeding from a wound in the head caused by a blow inflicted by complainant with a poker.—The bench dismissed the case. • __ How PIT DISASTERS ARE CAUSED.

At Newton, on Thursday, a case was heard in which a collier named George Edwards, of Haydock, was charged with breaches of colliery rules. Defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. Allen, of Messrs Preece and Ellis, Wigan, represented Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and said that on December 11, whilst working in the Pfincess Pit, at Haydock,defendant's safety lamp went out,and instead of taking it to the authorised place to be relit, he forced the lamp open, struck a match, and lit the lamp. There, were between sixty and seventy men in the mine, and a big explosion might have occurred. Messrs. Evans wished to press the case, andasked for the full penalty. The bench fined Edwards 40s. and costs in two cases, and hoped it would be a lesson to him.—Bernard Hopkins was fined 10s. and costs for not having c,arbonite in a cannister whilst in the mine at Haydock. Patrick Flanna,gan was fined 2s. Gd. and costs for taking a pipe down the mine; and William Cassidy, for a similar offence, was fined ss. in- cluding costs. INfr. Allen, of Messrs. div.head: INFLUENZA INCREASING.
div.p: INFLUENZA INCREASING.

The Influenza Epidemic is again spreading over the Country. The visitation is of a very prostrating nature, and the disease is certainly on the increase. The origin of the disease or rather the circumstances which bring it about is as mucha mystery as ever. You cannot trifle with Influenza. It undermines the Nervous System to a greater extent than almost any other disease, and it is Pneumonia that kills, and Pneumonia strikes the man who imagines he has only a mild form of Influenza, and can go about the street just as usual. It can hardly be doubted that the prevalence of Chest and Lung Complaints must be ascribed to the baneful influence of Influenza, whose after-effects so frequently take this form. It was a bad day for this Country when this malignant scourge first visited our shores. Year after year it has never since failed to revive at its due time, and to extort its tribute of human life. Having observed its ravages, and its dreadful effects upon the constitution on the occasion of its former visits, we , cannot but regard its recurrence with much fear, as a great many have not yet, if they ever will,regain their former health. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
Minor Cases. Warrington Borough Court.
FRlDAY—Before Mr. H. Roberta (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, Councillor John Roberts and Mr.

Hepherd. DELAPIDATED CORPORATION PROPERTY.-31r. S. Wilson, deputy town clerk, said he applied for an order to close five houses, 37a, 54, 58, and 60, Golbome-street, and 26a Queen-street. He was in a rather singular position as he appeared to prosecute and also to consent on behalf of the Corporation to the order. The pro- perty had been of considerable trouble to the Health Department for some time and had recently been pur- chased by the Corporation for street imnrovements. The condition of the property was such that the Cor- poration were advised that it would be almost impos sible to put it in repair. If the order vere -lade it would help the Corporation in a legal difficulty in con- nection with other property.—The order was made. AN OLD OFFMIDER.—Thomas Moran and Peter Scully were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Jackson's-court, Church-street, the previous-night.— Scully made his 32nd appearance and was fined 20s. and sts. Moran was fined ss. and costs. WOULD NOT PAY TEE PARE.—Robert Thompson ,IN:e road,was summoned for travelling on a Corporation tramcar and refusing to pay the fare.—Mr. S. Wilson, Deputy Town Clerk, prosecuted.—Robert Holloway, tram conductor, said the defendant entered a car at the Post Office and paid the fare from the Post Office to Rylands-street. When the car had passed Warrington Bridge witness asked him for the fare to Latchford and he refused to pay it, stating that he had already paid a penny. He said he wanted to get off at St. Mary- street and befare the car stopped he attempted to alight, but slipped and fell on the back of his head. He was under the influence of drink.—Mr. Wilson said the man received rather serious injuries and was uncon- scious for threequarters of an hour.—Defendant said he had not resided in the town long and did not know that he had to pay another penny to go from Rylands-street, to Latchford.—A fine of 10s. was imposed.—Mr.Hepherd suggested that it would be advisable to have notices in the cars giving the various stages and the fares required Mr. Wilson said he would mention the matter to the manager. IMPEDING TRAMWAY TRAFFIC.—George Leigh, a carter, of Knutsford was summoned for impeding traffic on the Latchford,tramway on December 28th.—Evidence was given to the effect that defendant drove a horse and lnrry in front of a car for about a quarter of a mile. The driver sounded the gong but defendant refused to drive to one side although there was room for him to do so. Defendant, who said the road was too narrow for him to drive to the side, was fined in the costs (12s).

div.head: First Warrington Starr Bowkett Building
div.p: First Warrington Starr Bowkett Building
Society.

The annual meeting of this society was held at the office, 14, Cairo-street, on Monday evening. In the unavuidable absence of Mr. R. Sutton (the chairman of the society), Mr. J. W, Hayward, IP., was voted to the chair. The Board of Management submitted their sixteenth annual rep)rt, from which it appeared that there had been a loss on the year's working of £l4 4s. 71d., thus reducing the undivided profit of the society to £261 10s. 21d. The report was adopted. In the discussion which took place it was ppinted out that the past year was the first for many years that the society had lost on the year's working. 'There was every prospect of a better result being obtained next year. Three directors retired, named Messrs. Joseph Owen, Robert Sutton and J. W. Hayward, and they were unanimously re-elected. The auditors, Messrs. E. Bradshaw and F. Pearson were also re-elected.— _ _
The meeting concluded with an acknowledgment of the Chairman's services.

div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING.
div.p: MUNICIPAL TRADING.
INQUIRY QUESTION STILL UNSETTLED, Tuesday Night's Interesting Debate. • THE MAYOR AND HIS POSITION. Painful Ending of the Council Meeting.

The all-important inquiry question still remains un- settled. The subject was re-introduced at the monthly meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening but a painful incident brought the proceedings to an abrupt close before a vote had been taken. From the large assembly of the public it would appear that interest in the question is unflagging, the portion of the Ohamber allotted to spectators being again crowded. As at pre- vious meetings the debate was closely followed, and the speeches frequently aroused audible expressions of ap- proval or otherwise. The Mayor's request for silence had a temporary effect,but later on,the audience seemed unable to restrain themselves and applauded or groaned as their feelings dictated. The subject of the inquiry, was introduced by the Mayor who moved the re-con- sideration of the matter. After a protest by Councillor Dodds the resolution was carried. Alderman Monks's resolution with regard to the inquiry was then consider- ed. At about ten‘tninutes to ten Councillor Pemberton I was addressing the meeting when a painful incident occurred. Councillor Baird was seen to fall forward in a fainting fit and had to be carried out of the Council Chamber amid some confusion. The Mayor,under these circumstances, considered that an adjournment would be advisable, and the Council decided to continue the dis- cussion at a special meeting to be held on the 20th instant. In the meantime Dr. Fox had been summoned by telephone and attended Councillor Baird, who,at his directions, was removed to a committee room, wherehe lay on a couch for some time. The doctor found him to be suffering from syncope, caused by the heated atmosphere of the room, the excitement of the debate, land a slight attack of illness during the previous Vow days. Ultimately, he was removed home in a cab. THE MAYOR AND HIS POSITION.
HE DEPRECATES AN INQUIRY EXTENDING OVER HIS MAYORALTY.
MOTION TO RECONSIDER THE QUESTION CARRIED.

The MAYOR moved the following resolution To re-consider the question of the inquiry into the alleged trading with the Corporation by members of the Council who have any interest in any firm,business or limited co in- pany,and to pass resolutions therdon or otherwise."' do so, he said,in order to facilitate the wishes,as I am informed, of many member sof the Council. I was not present when the resolution in question was adopted.but I understand it was only passed by a small majority of one, and that at a very late hour, and when many members of the Council had left or were not in their places. It is to I give an opportunity for re-considvation, if the Council so desire it, that I am asked to move the resolution. There are two points in the resolution which it is proposed to reconsider, to which I desire to call attention. First, to suggest an inquiry- implies that there is something wrong to inquire into, but if it is to be considered wrong for the Corporation to have transactions with any local firm or company in which any councillor may have shares, be they few or many, I say it is a mistake, and for thetown a very serious mistake, for the tend- ency is to drive from the Council the very men you wish to see there—the large manufacturers colliery owners, ironmasters, or bankers, in fact, all having any stake in the industries of the town and neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) Not only so, but it will drive works and manufacturers from your town, for if the Corporation boycott them because a councillor happens to have a few shares, they had better go elsewhere, and so you are driving your best friends away,and sending your rate- payers' money to other towns and depriving your Own' workmen of the bread they would otherwise naturally earn. But it is :useless enlarging, the facts are too self-evident. I am not saying this to deprecate an inquiry; far from it. If there is anything to inqpire into, it did not happen in my time, and I neither Wish to promote nor discourage it. Only this I may say,that I deprecate an inquiry extending over November, 1901, the date I had the honour of accepting the mayoralty, unless you have any grounds for suspicion, or suspicion without grounds, that any improper or irregular tran- sactions have occurred which call for inquiry. I have told you on more than one occasion that I. have had personal experience of all your committees except one,l the Gymnasium Committee, and from my personal ex-1 perience I know that on every committee' which I have attended, the business has been carried on honestly, honourably, and in a business-like and straightforward manner. Therefore, I object to the indignity of an in- quiry affecting my term of office, unless there are any allegations to make or special transactions to inquire into in which case I should bow to your authority, but I should consider myself no longer worthy to be your Mayor. (Hear, hear). It is not by restrictiong,be they ever so stringent, that we shall ensure honour and honesty in our Town Council, but it is by the ennobling sense of its own dignity, its own probity and high standard of character and honour inculcating a good moral tone and an atmosphere of purity and devotion to duty. Thus, and only thus, the esteem and confidence and the respect of our fellow citizens will be not only our due, but, in time, our certain inheritance. (Applause). Councillor ROGERS seconded. COUNCILLOR DODDS REGRETS TO JOIN ISSUE. COMPLIMENT TO THE MAYOR.

Councillor DoDDS said: I regret to have to join issue with you, Mr. Mayor, on this matter. A special adjourn- ment of the last Council meeting was made mainly for the discussion of this trading question, and, in conse- quence, about four hours were spent upon it onlythree weeks ago. , It is true a great deal of time was wasted in what was aptly described as "a personal white-wash- ing. exhibition." Councillor F. R. ROBERTS: It was a lie. Councillor DODDS (continuing) said: It is quite true that all that kind of thing was entirely out of place, and that it was not stopped was solely because of the bias of your deputy in the chair—l could say a good deal on that point, but I forbear. What I submit is,that the matter was very fully discussed, and after two close divisions in committee, the Council after resumption, carried practically unanimously my motion for a full and an exhaustive inquiry. Councillor F. R. ROBERTS : By means of a trick. Councillor Dopps(continuing) : I appreciate,Mr. Mayor, the position you take up in this matter. I believe it to reflect the utmost credit upon you, for everybody knows that if there is a gentleman in this district, aye, or in this country, who is of unimpeachable 'honour, who is moved by, and only moved by the purest of motives, you are that gentleman. May I, however, remind you of the fact, because it is the fact,that it was owing to the action of the Non-Trading Association, more than to anything else, that the unique and successful appeal to You to accept and to restore the dignity of the Mayor- alty Warrington was unanimously approved .outside this room, and finally almost unanimously confirmed by the Connell. Although you. are strictly and legally a member of this Council, we non-traders all look upon you as, above and apart from it,in regard to all such questions as that which has so stirred Warrington over the past eighteen months. You did not seek to come here, you do not seek to remain here; no one of my friends would think of even Suggesting that under such circumstances your position should be questioned. I have all along held the opposite. and I challenge any- one to find any words of mine that can bear a contrary construction. What I have desired, what those behind me have deAired, has been to create such a public senti- ment in Warrington, as should render it impossible for any man to enter this Council to grind his own axe, or when in; to dare to do so. I believe there is not a man in the Council who does not know, who does not see,what we want (and there are none so blind as those who won't see). T believe there '..is. not a man in this

Council who.do'es not believe and know that what we have publiclyimpeached has been going on in the past 10 or 15 years to an appalling extent. The public of Warrington believe this—wh tt, better proof could you want or could you have of that,than the polling at the November elections? The. humble and practically un- known acceptors of the "No trading" policy, some of whom sit near me, polled 3,536 votes against the com- bined opposition of 1,936. I include Mr. Shaw who received 127 votes in Bewsey Ward as a " No-trader" because he assured me at the outset, in the hearing of the Conservative secretary, he was primarily a "No- trader " and only in a secondary sense a Conservative.

T, therefore, am 'bold enough to -claim on behalf of the four " No-trading " members of this Council (now happily as a result of Mr. Lord's unopposed return for Town Hall Ward yesterday increased to five members), a considerable, a dominating voice as to the character and constitution of any committee of inquiry, and as to the width and depth of its operations. The motion carried at the last meeting by 13 of your eldcted members, against seven (for I do not consider the aldermen have any representative character whatever)—(laughter)--- that motion demanded the irreducible minimum of what those I represent will accept, and with all defer- ence to you, Mr. Mayor, I see no reason whatever for the reconsideration of the questionjof the inquiry, and I shall unhesitatingly vote against your motion. (Applause.) The DEPUTY-MAYOR, in referring to the conduct of the business at the last meeting, said he was entirely in the hands of the members, who agreed to go into com- mittee. That meant that a man could speak as often as he liked. Councillor F. R, ROBERTS remarked that Councillor Dodds had put his claim that his motion ought not to be rescinded, on the ground that the Council unani- mously passed his resolutton. He (Councillor Roberts) interjected that it was passed by means of a trick. He repeated that accusation. The Nuncil did not bona-

others with him. He was astounded to hetz afterwardl that the committee had re-constituted itself a Counci and passed this resolution.

Councilor DODDS : Unanimously. Councillor F. R. ROBERTS: I say that WAS a trick Continuing, he said it wa.S seen that members of the Council were leaving under the impression that the whole proceedings were over. The motion ought to be reconsidered, and when it was reconsidered he should have something to say about it. Councillor PEMBERTON supported what Councillor Dodds had said in reference to the Deputy-Mayor. It was quite true that the Council. having resolved itself into committee, the members could speak as often as they liked, but members who spoke repeatedly referred to the Council as their Parr. Hall, and went on to talk as if they were in Parr Hall. If they wanted to do that they should go to the expense of taking Parr Hall and face the puolic-r(Anplause from the public)—not the ' few people who could gather together in that small Council Chamber. In reference to Councillor F. R. Roberts's remark as to the motion being passed by means of a trick, it was rather astonishing. Considering that the members of the Non-Municipal Trading Com- mittee were new members of the Council, they might claim to say that they were not up to the tricks of the Council yet. (Laughter.) He had a distinct recollec- tion that some members of the Council did not leave the room but stood at the doorway and would not vote. He would like to refer to a personal matter which was introduced at the last meeting. Catincillor Peacock charged him with being a member of a firm which was selling bricks for the new baths extension. He (the speaker) did not think it was right at the time, but he did not contradict the statement as he had no evidence in regard to it. He Ind since made inquiries and found that all his firm's bricks, were stamped so that they would be able to recognize all the bricks sent out of the works.
The MAYOR : I think you are travelling from tho motion.
Councillor PEMBERTON: It is a personal explanation arising out of the motion. _ _
Cotincillor PEACOCK : I only asked who supplied the bricks and I don't think it requires arty more explana- tion.

. Councillor PEMBERTON : I found the firm has not supplied the bricks, but the Warrington Slate Company are the people supplying them. ("Oh" from the public.) Alderman BOLTON stated that Councillor Dodds had shown his power,and it was now for the Council to hold an inquiry which 'would satisfy everyone. Would the inquiry proposed be satisfactory? He thGught not. Councillor Dodds ought to leave the appointment of the committee of inquiry to the Town Council. (Laughter.) The voting on the resolution was proceeded with, and resulted as follows :

ALDERMAN MONKS' RESOLUTION. "NOTHING WORTH ENQUIRING INTO." TEIE TRADING OF MONKS HALL AND CO., LIMITED. THE ALDERMAN TALKS OF RESIGNING.

Alderman MONKS, moved: (1) "That the resolution proposed by Mr. Councillor Dodds, and passed at the last meeting of the Council, be and is hereby rescinded"; and (2) "That in order to give an opportunity for in- vestigating the charges re-_:ently made as to the trading that has taken place between the Corporation and mem- bers of the Council during the three years ending 9th November, 1901, a county court judge or other qualified legal gentleman of equal standing be elected and appointed by the Mayor, in consultation with the Town Clerk, to inquire into and report upon any charges sub- mitted to him by the Municipal Non-trading Associa- tion or any ratepayer of the borough." He said: I rise to propose the two resolutions standing in my name. I do so with some hesitation, and still more reluctance, because there appears to have been so much of the per , sonal element introduced, that the main principles and objects of the agitation seem at times to have been left completely out of consideration and ignored. The fact that my proposal to rescind the resolutions passed at the last meeting is coupled with,and includes a proposal that an inquiry be held, is in itself sufficient evidence that my action is not prompted by a mere desire to oppose or in any way thwart the wishes or efforts of those who have conducted this agitation. On the con- trary I have every sympathy with the objects of their association, in so far as they are likely to reduce all illegal and improper trading between the Corporation and any of its members, in any shape or forth whatever. I have, however, very strong objections to their methods and it is these and these alone, which have prevented me from givingillthem active support. There would be no diffieulty in suggesting a course of action which if the objects of the association had been merely to limit the trading as far as possible, would have brought about that result in six months time and without all the uproar and unpleasantness that has prevailed during the last 18 months. At the beginning of this agitation I interposed so far as to write Mr.'Norbury Williams, and stated "a large proportion of members of the Council would welcome any fair and reasonable inquiry," with what result you already know. If my letter had been replied to in the same spirit in which it was written I feel certain an inquiry would have followed imme- diately. I do not, however, blame Mr. Williams. He could only do what his informants and advisers allowed. Therefore the leaders of this Municipal Non-trading Association are responsible, and they alone for the failure to get an inquiry at the end of 1901; or early last year. To show that my sympathy with the objects of the association is no mere expression 0f approval, or an attempt to appear wise after the event, let me state what action T have taken in regard to the trading of my own firm. I was first elected a member of the Council in 1890. Prior to that time my firm used to trade with the Corporation direct, and continued doing so for some time lifter. It was in 1893 (nine years ago) that I saw or thought I saw possible complications in the future if this direct trading were allowed to continue. In order to be quite certain of my facts, a careful investigation of the company's ledgers has been made, and I find with one exception no goods have been supplied direct since September, 1893, for.which pay- ment has been made. The exception referred to is an item amounting to 4s. 7d. for goods supplied to the order of the Borough Surveyor in April, 1900. Since 1893 certain traders in town at times purchased goods from our company and supplied them to the Corporation, but in November,l9oo, after the disclosures made in Manchester in connection with Mr Higgin- botham's case, it seemed to me desirable to stop even , this indirect trading. I, therefore,and at once,did what ' was possible to stop it. so faras I could, without inter- fering with the business of third parties. Since that time there has been one case of indirect trading that I know of or have been able to trace, the amount involved being .£6 18s. Now it is not only that I have tried to stop all trading, whether direct or indirect, I have gone so far as to allow the company to supply goods to the Corporation for which no charge hag been made. It was a case of urgency when a very great deal was at stake. The goods had been ordered in ample time from a works in Staffordshire, but the makers failed to keep any of the numerous promises made. The goods could not then be got in time from any other firm in the country, and I allowed the work to be done by my own people, but made ne charge, because I was chairman of the committee. I think this is enough to show that my approval of the objects of the association is no mere expression of opinion, and having done so much it is not unlikely I am willing to go further still. Other mem- bers of the Council have, held the same opin- ions in regard to this trading question, not- ably the members of the Finance Committee. This was the one committee which could do more to deal with improper trading than any other, and I must say my colleagues have, in my opinion, risen to the occasion, and before the Municipal Non-trading Association was formed, or its promoters were heard of in Warrington, the committee had anticipated and taken active steps to improve the situation. Let me point out, however, there was no public opinion on this ques- tion until after the disc!osures in Manchester in October and November, 1900, and in the absence of such a strong opinion as now undoubtedly exists,it was very difficult for the Finance Committee to take a strong line without running the risk of possible misunderstandings with the committees and members concerned. To havetakenany step or adopted any course of action likely to lead to such a result did not appear to us likely to help on or , facilitate the general business of the Corporation, and so, at the risk of the work taking longer to complete, the Finance Committee thought it _better to try and bring about the reform by quieter methods. By a word here, a suggestion there, occasionally referring accounts back again with recommendations, and gentle but steady pressure all round, the committee had brought about such reforms as to put matters upon what I still think, and can only describe,as a satisfactory footing. So that when the disclosures were made in Manchester we could con- gratulate ourselves on having already accomplished ; what Manchester then found it necessary to do. This, however, is rather wandering from my resolution, but I am not aware that it has been said before, and tha pre- sent seemed to offer a suitable opportunity for putting in a word, on behalf of the much abused Finance Com- mittee. (Hear, hear.) Now as to my reasons for wish- ing to rescind the resolutionpassed at the last meeting I was not present during the discussion norat the voting I only stayed long enough to vote for Councillor Peacock's amended resolution agreeing to an inquiry and then, left under the impression there was no chance of Mr. Councillor Dodds's resolution being carried, and

that there would be another opportunity for saying something as to the precise form the inquiry would take. If there is to be an inquiry into the trading between the Corporation and firms in which members of the Council have been, or are, partners, or through limited com- panies in which they are shareholders, whether the trading is direct or indirect—it most surely imply that all such trading is either improper, or undesirable, or wrong. Otherwise there is no justification for the inquiry to be hold at all. It is now being said that the resolutions are not intended to apply to, small or com- paratively small shareholders in large companies. But where is the dividing line to be drawn and who is to drawa ? If members of the Council draw a line for themselves how are they to know if such a decision is , approved ofloutside ? Even if Mr. Councillor Dodds ' agreed to such a definition as would be satis- factory, what guarantee have we that he will , not change his opinion to-morrow or 'next year ' and start another agitation against the small shareholders in a large company ? Or what is to prevent Mr. Dodd's prototype in years to come starting a similar agitation? The risk of being so pilloried is one I am not prepared no ran. No, the principle is the same whatever be the amount involved, whether it is £l,OOO or only a penny. I contend that a resolution passed by this Council must be carefully considered by each member, to see how far it affects him individually. Our position and circumstances in relation to the Corporation differ so much from each other that what may be right for one member to do, may be wrong for another. The Mayor has decided the matter so far as he is concerned, and his decision seems to me the right one. I have tried to think the matter out so far as the resolution concerns me, and if it is retained, then I see no other course open but to send in my resignation. Let me give a single instance to show how it will work —and a concrete case explains better than any amount of talking. It is a case that may now exist for anything I know to the contrary. My company makes tubes and fittings, and these are purchased by a firm in town and stocked on their own premises. The firm in question may secure the contract from the Gas Committee for the year, and in the ordinary course supply goods made by my firm. I have no idea what are the require- ments of the Gas Committee, for I have never spoken to the Gas Works Engineer nor any member of the committee about it. I am, however, certain it forms only a very small percentage of the total trade done between us; Still the goods bear the registered mark of the company, and can be identified by any workman in the employ of the Gas Committee. Now such trading comes under the terms of Mr. Dodd's resolution, and therefore as a 'holder of shares in Monks, Hall and Company I am liable to be included in the proposed inquiry. I have no right to aak the firm in question what they do with the goods, and I must, therefore, decide between my company giving up their account, and so sacrificing the interests of my firm or resigning my position here. It does not require any consideration as to what my decision will be. Now for the form of the tribunal provided in Mr. Dodd's motion. Supposing the four members agree as to the fifth; what farther point of importance will such an inquiry bring out, and even if all are agreed upon a report, what value is to be placed upon their united opinion when so expressed? We know, or at any rate have a sufficient knowledge of what four out of the five may be likely to say,so that the opinion of the fifth is the only one that may be considered of any value to the ratepayers and the public generally. Then why go to the expense or burden the tribunal unnecessarily by adding four others whose opinions are sufficiently well known beforehand. Personally lam strongly against any inquiry of any kind whatever, for the simple reason that in my opinion there is nothing worth while inquiring into that is likely to repay the time, trouble and expense involved. It is, however.con- tended that the return of Mr. Dodds and Mr. Pemberton is evidence of the ratepayers' desire that an inquiry should be held. While Ido not admit this is so, because only a small proportion of the ratepayers were directly appealed to, I may be wrong in my opinion. There is no opportunity of putting it to the test, and I, there- fore, withdraw any further opposition to an inquiry, in the hope and expectation that by so doing I am helping to bring this unfortunate agitation to a close. I say ; unfortunate, because there is no doubt it has done the towna great amount of harm. How much, and for how 1 long will never be known, but I say this, and I say it In all seriousness after much reflection and considera- tion, that the agitation has already done more harm to the town than all the so-called illegal and immoral ; trading that is said to have taken place during the last ten years.
Councillor PEMBERTON : Question. Alderman MONKS: There is no questien about it. Councillor PEMBERTON : Perhaps not, in your own mind.

I —Alderman MONKS, continuing,rsaid : If instead of I spending so much time in demanding an inquiry into the I past, the promoters of this agitation had given one-half I or one-fourth of the time to formulating or elaborating I a reasonable and workable method of procedure in the' future in regard to this trading question, they would or might have done the town some good. So far as they have made any proposals, experience is already Ibeginning to show that they will not work and cannot therefore be adopted. So much, therefore, for the res- cinding of the resolutions. There is, however, another I feature in connection with Mr. Dodd's resolution it I seems necessary to refer to. The resolutions having been passed and placed on the minutes, surely some ! further step or action must be taken, and that at an I early date, the sooner the better. The natural step,and Indeed the only poSsible one is for the General Pur- poses Committee to do what is necessary to put the resolution into effect, and whose duty was it to see to this? Surely the individual who was responsible for Introducing the resolutions. I, therefore, attended the meeting of the General Purposes Committee in order to see what action 'Mr. Councillor Dodds pro- posed to take, and you may judge of my surprise to find that he was not even present at the meeting. (Hear, hear.) Here is an example of a gentleman taking upon himself the responsibilities of a Town Councillor, securing the passing of a resolution of what is likely to prove such a revolutionary kind involving as it does the possible resignation of the Mayor (whom everybody admits is in no way implicated), a resolution that seems likely to temporarily bring the business of the town to a standstill. Here, t repeat, is a case of a member tak- all this responsibility and then shirking the consequences by staying away from a meeting. However, one cannot be altogether surprised at his action, or rather want of action, at the crucial moment. Councillor DODDS : May I explain? The MAYOR: You will have an opportunity later on. Alderman MONKS: It is all on a par with his behaviour at the early meetings of the Pinance Committee, when he sat there taking notes of the proceedings, but de- clined to take any part in the work of the committee, or even venture to express an opinion upon the matters under discussion. I wonder if the 600 and odd ratepayers who voted for Mr. Dodds realized when recording their votes they were sending as their representative one who to use his own words, "had soma doubt as to the legality of his position, as • a member of the Council." (Applause.) However, I coming back to the meeting of the General Purposes Committee, the situation seemed to me so critical as not to warrant any further delay,and failing, Mr. Dodds, I took it upon myself to bring---or rather you, Mr. Mayor, introduced the matter)—the matter forwitrd, Iwith the result that I am now submitting my views in regard to the whole question. Now as to the form of • inquiry I propose. You will notice the words "as to I trading" do not limit the inquiry in any way. Whether I legal, illegal or immoral, they can all be submitted to the judge, and it seems to me,better to let him draw his own distinctions, and say .which are fit and proper cases for inquiry. As to the time limit, three years ending November 9, 1901,the Mayor has already made a definite pronouncement as to the result of his observations during the period since that date. I feel that his word Iwill be generally accepted by e*erybody, and therefore, no inquiry seems necessary in respect of the period since the date named. Equal confidence will be felt in any selection the Mayor may make as to who shall con- duct the inquiry. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Neither the Council nor the Municipal Non-trading Association should have the controlling voice in the selections. (Hear, hear.) We are all either plaintiffs or defendants, and, therefore, ought( to be glad to submit our differ- ences to an outside and independent authority, selected by some one individual who is not directly interested, and, therefore, will be impartial. = Then the concluding portion is so worded that any single individual ratepayer may come forward. Nothing could be wider than that. The judge will, of course, arrange the order of procedure, and the intention of my resolution includes the produc- tion of any book or document that may be called for. I feel this, however, that if the inquiry is to be worth what it will cost, and that will be no inconsiderable sum, someone must come forward with something .definite. Here is the opportunity. Vague statements and insinuations have been flying around long enough. The Municipal Non-Trading Association is responsible both for them and the agitation. They must have some facts and figures in their possession to justify their statements. Let them come forward with such as they have. If they want more, Councillor Pemberton, who ha i had such a long experience of investigating the Corporation accounts, will be able to get all that is wanted, for,as a member he has the run of all accounts, minute books, and everything else requisite. Let them submit what facts and figures they have, in their pos- session to justify all this hubbub which they have created. If the judge decides in their favour I for one will pledge myself to assist them to obtain a more ex- tended inquiry. I could have said a great deal more, but I think I have already said sufficient to show the , need for rescinding the last resolution, and, I hope also, sufficient to ensure the acceptance and passing of the resolution I now put before you. I hav6 tried to deal with the whole que3tion in a strictly impartial manner,
The Most Nutritious.

withoevery desire to bring about a solution that, while being satisfactory to the contending parties, will also satisfy the general public, and let the matter drop into oblivion. What I feel is, that so much solicitude as to the past is out of place, and too much like trying to lock the stable door after the horse is stolen. The interests of the town are suffering seriously, but until this agitation is out of the way we cannot give the busi- ness that thought or consideration which it demands. (Hear, hear, aud applause). THE FORM OF THE INQUIRY. COUNCILLOR ROBERTS AND "OLD WIVES'

TALES."

Councillor F. R. ROBERTS seconded the motion, and said he would like to repeat the two arguments he brought forward at the last meeting. If there was one thing they wished to avoid it was being made fools of, and he said emphatically that the resolution of Mr Dodds did make fools of them. It asked the inquiry to do what it had no power to do, viz.: administer the oath and investigate sub-contracting. Councillor DODDS : On oath or otherwise! Councillor ROBERTS :Then.why not leave it out?
Councillor DODDS
We will have it if we can.

Councillor ROBERTS: I object to il;i7s Council being made to look foolish simply because Councillor Dodds insists on this sacred script of his being passed verbatim et literatim. Proceeding to refer to the questionof sub- contracting—the trading going on between contractors and members of the Council—Councillor Roberts said that no court of inquiry, however constituted, had any power whatever to examine the books of members of the Council. Therefore, why ask the inquiry to do it? What he objected to most of all, however, was the totally absurd constitution of . the Board of Inquiry. (Hear, hear.) The Non-Trading Association desired to nomi- nate two out of four, and as they could also, it appeared, carry the vote of the Council, they might by that means obtain the selection of the four nominees. If they per- I sisted in this unfair, un-English, and unjust resolution he would have nothing to do with the Board of Inquiry at all, and*if there were any charges against him at the inquiry they (the accusers) would be served with writs within 24 hours. (Applause and laughter.) He was not going to submithis morality to any four gentlementhat the members of the Non-Trading Committee would nominate. Another thing ! Let them assume that they had got the four nominees. Unless these four men were skilled in the admission and rejection of evidence, who could tell what old wives' fables, grandmothers' tales and lies could not be poured into the ears of these men? (Hear, hear.) How were they to know what was admissible and what Was not? (Applause.) How were their (the Councillors') rights to be safe- guarded? What was there to provide that they would be able to put their case before the tribunal ? (Hear, hear.) There was nothing in the resolution to secure a proper hearing to those members of the Council charged with illegal and immoral trading. He would not coun- tenance in any way an inquiry on these lines. He wished to say, in conclusion, that a great deal had been said— rightly and properly—about the high and noble stand the Mayor hadtaken. What he waited to know was this: Why these gentlemen who so properly had given the Mayor credit,had not given credit to some of them who not only did not vote ion committees upon which they sat, but who were not even members of any com- mittee whatever that gave contracts to any firm in which they had an interest? (Applause.) Why had these people not done them that justice? (Hear, hear.) Why did they find a newspaper like the "Guardian" stating that shady things had been done within the last twelve months. The gravamen of the charge was that ,they were using their personal influence upon the Council to secure their own ends. If the editor wrote these remarks and included him(Mr. Roberts), he accused him (the 2ditor) of telling a de- liberate and malicious falsehodd. These words were absolutely untrue and he challenged him to prove one iota of the charge. Their accusers would not give them one word of credit. , These gentlemen had shown their I personal animus all through and unless therewas an inde- pendent tribunal, they would not get justice to them- selves, the town would not accept the verdict, and the whole thing would have to be done over again. He agreed with Alderman Monks that the only proper person was a judge learned in the admission of evidence, ; impartial, and who could be relied upon to decide ques- -1 tions of legality, Morality and integrity. (Applause.)
COUNCILLOR DODDS OBJECTS TO THE MOTION. A MORAL, NOT A LEGAL QUESTION.

Councillor DODDS, in replying to the statement of Alderman Monks, respecting his (Councillor Dodds) non- appearance at, the General Purposes Committee, said he did not know the rules of the General Purposes Com- mittee. He thought it was the duty of the Town Clerk to bring the matter before that committee and not the duty of a private member. He would like the Town Clerk's opinion concerning that point. The TOWN CLERK: I say it is not my duty to bring the subject before the committee. Councillor DODDS : Very well as I did not know that, I think Alderman Monks will acquit me of any desire to shirk my responsibilities.

Alderman SUTTON: It was your duty to know. • , Councillor Dorms: If I had known that I had to introduce the subject at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee I would have been present! I had a most important engagement at Liverpool, which I could not very well avoid, and seeing that the subject was not wit on the agenda, I thought I would not be required. I hope this explanation is acceptable to every- body here. Continuing, Councillor Toodds3 said he was desirous of an inquiry into the trailing transactions of the Corporation,so that everything would be found out and reported to the Council. The public would then be able to see what trading had been done, and judge the position with the full facts before them. The matter had arisen out of the Higginbottom case. That struck him as a matter of such importance that they ought to see whether anything was going on in that Council. He went up to London and . consulted there with a menaber of.the late Liberal Government of the highest standing. He told him (Mr. Dodds) that it would probably take 20 years to get the law altered as it affected municipal trading. The best course was to hold meetings and expose these things. The object in view was so to effect public sentiment as to make it impossible for any man to come into the Council to serve his own ends or make money for himself. He objected to the motion because it was dishonest, because it sought to evade the real issue, and because it in no sense whatever met the reasonable demands of the ' ratepayers as made in the many great public meetings which had been held, and through the Noyember elec- tions. He objected to the reduction of the time over which an inquiry should be held. He objected to the proposed tribunal, because it was a moral and not a legal question which had to be sub- mitted to it, and because four or five good business men including one or two accountancy experts were the best persons to find out and report to the ratepayers upon what theylwanted to know,that was the amount of improper and immoral trading, if any, and whether legal or not, that had been done by each and every alderman and councillor during at least six financial years past. He objected to the selection of a tribunal by the Mayor and the Town Clerk for obvious reasons, and he objected to the ridiculous and unreal proposal as to the submission of charges by the Munici- pal Non-Trading Committee, before they had had any opportunity of getting up their full evidence from the books and from thelemployes of the Corporation.Helnid said that this motion was dishonest. What he meant , was that it sought to substitute for the inquiry which the ratepayers desired an entirely different inquiry. They wanted a full inquiry into all the trading which had I been done by members of the Council either through firms or through limited companies over the past six years. The people wanted an inquiry to discover all the " shady things" which one member of the Council had told them had gone on. - .

Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS: I did not say it. Councillor DODDS : I am only referring to the report. Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS: In one paper. Councillor DODDS (continuing) said the motion of Alderman Monks,soughtto narrow any inquiry into one which should simply result in a lawyer telling us that the few cases of trading through companies which the Non-TntdingiAssociation had ferretted out before any of its members came into the Council had been legal. In other words, the people behind him had demanded an inquiry which should discover all The improper trading of aldermen and councillors, while Alderman Monks wanted the opinion of a lawyer as to whether the trad- ing of members through companies was legal or illegal. They knew that much of the trading had been legal: what they wanted was to expose all improper trading. His motion would have effected what the ratemers wanted. Alderman Monks' motion was nothing more nor less than a shirking of the issue and he bhould vote against it. (Applause from the ratepayers at the end of the room.) Councillor P EMBERTON observed that Alderman Monks had objected to the methods of the non-trading com- mittee, but he had never taken the opportunity of attend- ing a meeting of the committee and told them person- ally the methods which would have brought about the inquiry in the speedy time he predicted. When the agitation was commenced they had no idea that it would be necessary to return members to the Council to obtain the object they had in view. They were of opinion that there were many members who would force an inquiry.

One or the greatest difficulties was the compact between! the two political parties. (Hear, hear.) He failed to see how it as possible to purify the Council whilst the political compact existed. He thought it was most unfair, ungentlemanly, and im- proper for Alderman Monks to speak as he had done in regard to Councillor Dodds and the General Purposes Committee. He insinuated that Councillor Dodds would not" face up." If the Council considered the position that Councillor Dodds had taken up, the odium which had been cast on him, and the amount of pressure which had brought upon him to forego the agitation, he thought they would give him credit for not running away from the General Purposes Committee. There was nothing in that Council to run away from. Alderman Monks said there was no public opinion on the coutmcts question before the Higginbottom case. He (Council- lor Pemberton) did not agree with him. The town had been seething with discontent for years. It was common talk and common knowledge that the trading and con- tracting had gone on. The members of the Council knew it, and it was only drawing a red herring across the path when they said it had not. Alderman Monks admitted that it had gone on but said it would not be in he interest of the public to have it investigated. It would perhops. not be in the interests of those who had carried it on. There could be no harm in an investiga- tion and he did not object to the inquiry embracing all' the members, himself included. Councillo DODDS : I don't object. _

Councillor PEMBERTON said Councillor Dodds' pro- position was that everything should be investigated and the public and the Council could judge to what ex- tent the trading had gone on. He (Councillor Pember- ton) was quite willing to leave the public to judge. In regard to his connection with Messrs. Artingstall, if the town said he should not be in the Council he was per- fectly willing to leave it. Councillor PEACOCK: You will have to do if they say so, Councillor PEMBERTON i We will see what the public say about that. (Loud "Hear, hear" from the public.) Continuing, Councillor Pemberton said he was sure he NYas expressing Councillor Dodds' sentiments when he said that he did not cast any reflection on any Coun- cillor who had traded moderately with the *Council. ("Oh's" from the Council.) He was afraid those people who "drew the red herring "were more implicated than many people thought. They seemed to be so anxious not to have an investigation. Alderman SUTTON: Everybody is most anxioug to have a proper investigation. Councillor PEMBERTON You seem to be most anxious not to have it. Continuing, he said Alderman Monks referred to the opportunity he (the speaker) had of investigating all the books. He rather questioned that,and he wanted to say that the position he had been placed in since he entered the Council was that he dare not individually go and investigate the books. In fact, he would not.
At this point, Councillor Baird was seized with a fainting fit and was removed from the chamber.

The MA.YOR suggested an adjournment of the discus- sion. It was nearly ten o'clock and he was afraid he would not be able to stanl it much longer. The DEPUTY. MAXOR suggested that if the meeting were adiourned the gentlemen who had spoken that night should not be allowed to speak again on the subject.

Alderman SUTTON proposed that the meeting be ad- journed for a fortnight. Councillor WILKINSON seconded the motion which was carried. The MAYOR said it should be understood that those gentlemen who had alrouly spoken would not be allowed to speak again on the resolution. The Council then rose. •

div.head: TO GO TO SCHOOL. Children Suffer in Bad Weather.
div.p: TO GO TO SCHOOL. Children Suffer in Bad Weather.

"In spite of the longer walks," said a school Board officer " the attendance at country schools is better than in towns"; but one fears that this entails suffering on the little ones. In this connection the "Northwich Mercury "reports a visit to Burston, near Diss, where Mrs. Witherley,of Hill House gave a personal illustration. "My daughter, Mend Elizabeth, is thirteen," she said. "She walked to school, a mile away, until about three years ago last May, when she became ill, and would probably be a helpless cripple to-day but for Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. She was not able to walk, and ate hardly at all. I used to carry her in my arms. If accidently touched she screamed with pain. I took her to the Norfolk and Norwich Hospital, where the doctors said she was suffering from hip disease, and wanted her to undergo an operation, but I refused.

"But," continued Mrs. Witherley, "we read in a book an account of a little boy cured of hip disease by Dr. Williams' pink pills, and decided to try whether they would do my daughter any good. "Before she had taken half a box she began to eat better, and her leg was perceptibly stronger. She has not yet taken eight boxes, and you can see for yourself how active she is getting. She is better in general health than she has been for years, and always seems to' be wanting something to eat. For three years I had to drive her about in an invalid chair, but this is now used for only very long distances. She is quite free from pain now." When diseases so severe are cured, it is no wonder that minor ailments—indigestion, bile, rheumatism, and bronchitis—yield to a few doses of the same pills. Dr. Williams' medicine company, Holborn-viaduct, London. send the pills post free for two shillings and ninepence, six boxes thirteen and nine. It is important to obtain genuine pills, bearing Dr. Williams' name: substitutes (which are sometimes pushed) never cured anyone. On another page of this issue will be found an interesting article on the use of the pills in preventing chills and influenza. A.question often asked is, "Flay these pills be given to children?" They may. For young children the dose is one-third of a pill ; children over ten may take half a pill. They can be cut with a knife, or may be dissolved in water if necessary.

div.head: PUBLIC HOUSE TRUST. Criticism by Warrington Temperance
div.p: THE PUBLIC HOUSE TRUST. Criticism by Warrington Temperance
Women.

At the meeting of the Warrington Branch of the British Women's Temperance Association, held at Bold- street, Wesleyan Vestry on Tuesday, evening, Mrs. Simpson, of Bewsey-road, read a paper against the Public House Trust. Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore, presided. In the course of her paper, Mrs. SIMPSON said she spoke against the Public House Trust not that she found the second condition worse than the first but that it was only a stepping aside, it was not a progressive movement. It appeared as though intoxicants were being placed within easy access of all classes so that those who would withstand the temptation had it forced upon their sight in places where they must go and those who had the least hankering for and were not troubled with qualms of conscience could take it without " infra-di bonitatus.". She, in com- pany with another lady visited the house in Bridge- street, now under the management of the Public House Trust Company. As they entered there was every appearance of an hotel with two rooms for the men to sit in, but upstairs was not so public-house looking there-being a private dining-room and a public one, the latter to seat about 22. Mrs. Simpson proceeded to explain the objects of the trust, and gave Earl Grey's own aC o o unt of the genesis of the scheme. From reading, she said, she found that drunk- enness or drinking had increased in the towns where this new scheme had been put into prac- tice. Anumber of men of position and even clergymen took an interest in the trade, which made it appear all the more innocent and young men were lured into it with the idea that it would be a good thing for the com- munity. Whilst in some towns they could point to good that had been done by the profits, the evil would far out- weigh it. She quoted from a paper read before the United Methodist Free Churches annual assembly at Leeds that no method of regulating or managing the distributon of alcoholic liquor would alter its power to do evil. The management theory seemed very much like the proverbial red herring thrown across the path of , temperance sentiment; and was likely to with- draw their efforts from the consideration of the evil. Socialists approved of it, hoping it would lead to schemes of municipalisation : politicians welcomed it as a means of staving off measures of drastic and effective reform and self-indul- gent Christians liked the idea, as it did not necessitate any self-denial on their part. But intelligent reformers, who had realised the practical fruits of total abstinence, and the marked success of prohibition, would not relax ' their efforts to obtain power for the people, not to manage but to veto out of existence this nefaripus traffic, which no aristocrat or ecclesiastic supervision could ever arkke clean or safe or wholesome. (Applause). Miss DUTTON considered-thnt if all the public-houses were managed on the lines and in the spirit of those who designed the scheme they might be of some advantage to those who had been accustomed to take a good den of drink. The great weakness was that the scheme seem- ed to give the public-house a soft of gentility and attractiveness to those who would otherwise keep outside public-houses. An interesting discussion followed, and Mrs. Simpson was thanked for her paper.

Child Fatally Scalded. At noon, on Wednesday, Mr. BriL2ju)use conducted an inquiry at Warrington relative to the dejth of Arthur Burge, three years of age, who resided with his parents at 10, Philip-street. Whilst the child's mother was engriged washing last Friday a pan of boil h ing water, which was on the lire, Was upset. The contents scalded the child about the face and tins. The child was taken to the Infirmary and died there on Saturday last. A verdict of " Accident-a; death " was returned.

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Service for Young People.

In accordance with a long-standing custom, the first Sunday morning of the New Year was devoted to a service for young people at Wycliffe Congregational Church. The preacher for the occasion was Mr. J. A. Yonge, M.A. (son of the Pastor of the church and Principal of Northern Congregational School, Silcoates, Wakefield). Suitable hymns were sung and the service concluded with a distribution of Bibles to the members of the pastor's catechumen class. The preacher based his discourse on Nehemia.h's -appeal his people at Jerusalem "Let us rise up and build !" After relating the circumstances which led to Nehe- miah's patriotic conduct in building the wall of Jerusalem, the preacher urged his hearers to be builders of character. The highest character, he pointed out was the Christian character, and Christ was the standard and Source of the noblest possible character. He wduld ask them to build this character and let conscience speak U the imperative mood to them—ln distributing the Bibles to the members of his class, the Rev. John \rouge enlarged on this theme and expressed the hope that each recipient would be from that day a character builder. The catechumen class has been in existence at Wycliffe for 22,years and is open to young people who have attained the age of 15 years.—At the evening ser- vice, the pastor preached on the Wycliffe motto for 1903, "One is your Master, even Christ."

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

Mr. Robert Nelson, of Sankey-street presided at the meeting of this society on Sunday, and referred to the Pleasure and satisfaction which was derived from Phristian service. .He expressed the hope that the corn- ing year wozild be a successful one, morally and piritually.—Mr. J. A. Yonge, M.A., deliveredan address in which he dealt with the -thief purpose of P.S.A. work and how they could best achieve the object they had before them. Their principal object, he said, was to bring men to know by personal experience that blessed liberty wherewith Christ made men free. Whilst admit- ting that a great deal needed to be done to improve the surroundings under which men lived, it was also necess- ary to bear in mind that men needed to be made better lit to live, and tills could only be done by Christian influences. He referred to the value of P.S.A. work in this direction, and said if the society was to accomplish its purpose it could only do so by hard work, self- sacrifice, and by " meaning business." Mr. Yonge pro- ceeded to speak of the successful propaganda work which was done by the Wakefield P.S.A. Society, of which he was president, and commended the work of their invitation band for imitation by the Wycliffe Society.—Mr. Hassan sang two solos in an effective manner.—ln referring to the forthcoming Penrhyn concert, the Rev. John Yonge commended the cause of the quarrymen as being worthy of the support of all who valued the liberty of workingmen, and the comfort of their wives and families. He firmly believed in this case that the men were right and the master wrong.—lt yeas announced that four new members had joined,bring- mg up the membership to 562.

div.head: SOME ASPECTS OF WINTER.
div.p: SOME ASPECTS OF WINTER.
We loved the Spring's expanding leaves, The bloom of summer flowers; Nor lows the mellow fruit and sheaves That crowned the Autumn hours.
But all are gone, and now one sees A. changed world in view— Deserted fields and naked trees, With skies of sombre hue.

Yet when full draped in Winter's snow The silent landscape lies, No scene more beautiful we know Beneath our English skies. - Ali, then from some extended lawn, While stars are ling'ring still; We love to watch the blush Of dawn Creep o'er the distant hill. Nor love we less the noontide stroll Through frost-encrusted ways; Whose breath revives the weary soul, And fills the heart with praise. Then 0, what glory gilds his nights, When clouds are rolled away; And heaven unfolds the world of lights We never see by day!
And when he takes his wildest form, With winds at his command, What grandeur marks the rolling storm That lashes sea and land!
J. H. W. CLINDINNING January, 1903.

div.head: LEAGUE,---FIRST DIVISION.
div.p: THE LEAGUE,---FIRST DIVISION.
WARRINGTON v. SWINTON.

There were 5,000 spectators at Warrington on Satur- day to witness the game with Swinton. Owing to recent rain the ground was very heavy, but the weather was satisfactory-. Both teams had absentees, Swinton being without Valentine, Morgan and Samuel, while Warrington missed Isherwood and Harris. The teams were composed as follows; 1 Warrington—Knight, back; Fish, Dickenson, Hallam, and Edwards, three-quarter backs; Burgess and Hocken- hall, half backs; Boardman, Swift, Coleman, Roberts, Edmondson, Morrison, Harmer,and Naylor, forwards. Swinton—Chorley, back; Hampson, Wallwork, J Taylor and Lewis, three-quarter backs; Williamson and C. Taylor, half backs; Cheetham, Yates, Evans, Tickle, Berry, Pomfret, Barnett, and Preston, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Salford ; touch judges, Messrs. Brimelow, Salford, and J. Gatley, Altrincham. Swift started for Warrington, and Lewis made a brilliant effort to score, but was sent into touch. Swinton subsequently gained possession, but Knight, the home back, kicked into touch. Fish got the ball, but was tackled before any opening showed itself. Hocken- hall put in useful work for Warrington, but a mark stopped progress. The Swinton backs started a ve;y promising movement, but Edmunds spoiled it by pulling up Wallwork. Swinton pressed, and Preston made two unsuccessful shots at goal. Half-time arrived with no score.

Barnett re-started. Warrington'obtained the ball, but a good effort was spoiled through Dickenson slipping. Hockenhall put in a splendid run, but had the misfortune to fall when nearing the line. Several exciting scrummages took place, but Warrington could not get through. Swinton took matters to their opponents' quarters, and continued to press. After some open play and kicking from end to end, Dickenson almost got over. Swinton were penalised, Fish's kick at goal failing. Warrington made another, rush, but were stopped near the line, and time came with no score.
HOW FEVER IS SPREIID.
Neglectful Warrington Mothers Fined.

On Friday at Warrington a respectably-dressed young woman named Ellen Sinipson, of Turner- street, was 'fined 10s. and costs for failing to notify a case of scarlet fever. Defendant's child was discovered in the peeling stage. and there were nine people in the house. _ _

Dr. Gomall, medical officer of health, stated that there Dr., not the slightest doubt that this case had been a source of infection to people in the neighbourhood. The Deputy Town Clerk said it was perfectly useless for the Corporation to attempt to isolate cases if people were going to act in a reckless manner in not reporting cases. Georgina Shaw, Cliff-lane Bridge, Knutsfoid-road, Grappenhall, was summoned for wilfully exposing her child John whilst suffering from scarlet fever. Dr. C ,rnall said he wascoming to Warrington from Latchford by the car, and he noticed a child along with the defendant, which showed symptoms of scarlet fever. When the terminus was reached he examined the child ndA found that it was in the peeling stage. s fine of 20s. including costs, was imposed.
The Examiner, Friday, January 9, 1903.

div.head: WIDNES v. RUNCORN.
div.p: WIDNES v. RUNCORN.

These old rivals met at Widnes' before 3,000 specta- tors. The home team at once attacked. Peacock was given a chance, but he spoiled it by knocking on. Houghton kicked down the field, and Tilley returned; but Price failed to gather the ball, and Hughes dribbled over the line for Rispan to drop on it. Tilley failed at goal. Half-time score :—Widnes I try (3 pointe), Run- corn nil. Early in the second half Widnes attacked,but Houghton cleared. After a lot of neutral play Runcorn attacked strongly, and for fully ten minutes the home team were penned on the line. Jolley and Richardson tried hard to break through, but failed. On two occa- sions Jolley kicked with rare judgment, and each time Bown was applauded for marking when sorely pressed. Result :—Widnes 1 try (3 points), Runcorn, nil. Teams: Widnes,—Tilley, back; Hughes Rispan, Bown, and Peacock, three-quarter backs; ally and Taylor, half backs ; Aspey, Power, Cockram, Leyshon, Riley, Rigby, Curtis, and Webster, forwards. Runcorn.—Houghton, back; Dutton, Price, Butter- worth, and Jones. three-quarter backs ; Richardson, and Jolley, half backs; Walker, Farmer Woods, Gayter, W. Houghton, S. Langley, Higgins, and Williams, forwards. Referee, Mr. B. Ashton, Oldham. Touch judges, Messrs. E. Elliott, Birkenhead, and J McGowan, Brough- ton.
BRADFORD v ST HELENS.

This 'latch at Park Avenue only attracted about 3,000 spectators. Bradford were short of Ward, Mosby, and Eagers, the latter pair in consequence of accidents— Mosby a broken nose and Eagers a crushed finger. The opening was slow, but mainly in Bradford's favour. half-time :—Bradford 1 goal and two tries (8 points), St. Helens 1 goal (2 points). On the change of ends everything went in Bradford's favour. Marsden, Murgatroyd, and Dunbavin dribbled from the visitors' "25 "to the line, where the latter scored, no goal being kicked. From passing between Foster and Marsden, Sinton put on a clever try,Broadley being unable to place the goal. Result :—Bradford 1 goal and 4 tries (14 points), St. Helens 1 goal (2 points.) OLDHAM iv. HULL. Played at Watersheddings, before about 5,000 specta- tors. One of the first items was a splendid attempt at goal almost from mid-field by Ferguson. At length S. Lees received from the scrimmage, and handed on to Cash, who used his speed to good effect, rounding Parry and Jacques, and scoring. Just before time Franks was penalised near the posts, and S. Lees easily placed the ball over the bar. Oldham "thus won a game that was too full of scrimmaging and kicking into touch to be interesting. Final :—Oldham one goal one try (5 points), to Hull nil.

div.head: HUNSLET v. SALFORD.
div.p: HUNSLET v. SALFORD.

The Parkside ground, Htmslet, was the venue of this encounter, and something like . 7,000 people witnessed the game. A splendid piece of passing between Hast- ner, Messer, and Lomas resulted in Bell scoring, and then towards the close Salford did pretty much as they liked. Lomas twice ran over, and on the first occasion he was allowed practically to walk right between the posts, whilst his other try was scored from near the centre. Result :—Salford two goals and four tries (16 points), to Hunslet one goal (2 points).

div.head: BATLEY V. WIGAN.
div.p: BATLEY V. WIGAN.

In the first half Batley had the advantage of both slope and wind, but their show fora long time was any- thing but encouraging, the form displayed by Wigan being verypraisewortliy. Then Davies landed a penalty goal. The next item was a fine burst up the field by, Rouse for Wigan, but Batley now assumed the aggres- sive, and practically held the upper hand to the end of the game. Judge scored, and Davies placed two penalty goals before the interval. Batley won by 3 goals 1 try (9 points), to nil.

div.head: BROUGHTON RANGERS v. LEIGH.
div.p: BROUGHTON RANGERS v. LEIGH.

Played at Broughton. There was no scoring beforp the interval, but in the second half the Leigh men bungle& badly on their own line, and Scott scored, W James kicking a goal. Result :—Broughton Rangers Ono goal one try (5 points), to Leigh nil.

div.head: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. HALIFAX
div.p: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. HALIFAX

At Hull on Saturday. At the time of the start a strong south-west wind was blowing, and the ground was rather slippery, owing to the heavy downpour a few hours earlier. The visitors at the outset pressed heavily, and Barry getting possession from a" scrum," threw to Morfitt, who dodged his opponents and passed to West, who put on full speed; and coming to Little dived clean under him and scored a try in the corner. Kemp's attempt at goal was a failure. There was keen play on both sides after this, but the home team had the best of matters. Barry tried to drop a goal, but the ball struck one of the visitors, and the attempt failed. Read at once got possession of the ball, and careered over the line, Rigg and Hadwen trying In vain to step him. Kemp took the goal kick, but failed, the score at the end of the first_ half being : Rovers two tries (6 points).

to Halifax nothing. Both teams played a good ga:me,and although the Rovers prevented Halifax from scoring they were unable to add to their half-time total, the game ending :—Rovers two tries (6 points), to Halifax nil.

Mr. niroh,ai :R was an act of great cruelty to bring it away. Prisoner, continuing, said it was through one of the clergy, who was continually on his doorstep arguing. When he got the child home he never,saw the priest after.

The Chairman : Do you say that, one of the clergy pressed you to take the childaway from Mrs.Rylatt ? The Female Prisoner : It Father Mercer, from St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street. The Male Prisoner: It was through him that the child was brought home, and no one else. The Chairman : That is a species of priestly intoler- ance that ought to be put an end to. Mr. Birchall : The portraits of the child show a most horrible contrast.

The Chairman,in announcing the magistrates' decision said he thought it was a most unfortunate thing that the priest interfered. He thought it was most repre- hensible on the part of any minister or priest to inter- fere in that sort of way. The decision of the benchwas that the male prisoner should go to gaol for three months. The children would go to the Workhouse. The Bench dismissed the sister, because they believed she was utterly incapable of managing the house and look- ing after the children. (To the male prisoner.) Take my advice, and don't let the priest interfere any more than you can help in your own household.

div.head: ALLEGED "PRIESTLY INTOLERANCE."
div.p: ALLEGED "PRIESTLY INTOLER- ANCE."
Singular Statement in a Warrington Neglect Case.

div.head: Magisterial Comments.
div.p: Magisterial Comments.

A singular statement which occasioned magisterial comment was made by a prisoner in a child neglect case at the Warrington Police Court on Monday. Tho mas and Mary Cullen brother and sister, residing at 20, Wellington-street, appeared before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates on the charge of neglecting six chil- dren in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the INT:S.P.C.O and stated that Thomas Cullen was a widower, and his sister was his housekeeper, and had been for a consider- able time. The male prisoner was a labourer at the St. Helens Cable Works, and was earning 245. a week. He was formerly employed at the Castle Rubber Works, where he earned 28s. a week. One of his lads brought in B.s. a week. Unfortunately, in January last the male prisoner lost his wife, leaving him with the care of six children, but a good woman, named Mrs. Rylatt, living in Greenall-street, came forward, and offered to take charge of the baby, and to bring it up. The child was then a month old. The male prisoner consented,and the child was kept by Mrs. Rylatt for six months. Mr. Browne then produced a photograph of the child, show- ing it to be in a perfectly healthy condi- tion when in charge of Mrs. Rylatt, and handed it to the Bench. Continuing he said that at the end of six months the man insisted upon having the child back. It was sent back in August last to the I house of the prisoners, but later on, in consequence of it (having to be taken to the Infirmary to beattended to, a ! complaint was made to Inspector Hackett, who went with Sergeant Evans to the house in Wellington-street. They found a most deplorable state of affairs. The child was sucking some sour food from a bottle and was in a shocking condition. Inspector Hackett at once sent for Dr. Peacocke, who ordered the child to be taken to the Workhouse Infirmary. Mr. Browne handed the Bench a photograph of the child in its present condition, and said the baby weighed only 81, lb instead of about 191 b. I There werelonly two cups, one saucer and a basin in the ! house for nine people. The other children were vermin- ous, and Dr. Peacocke described the house as being unfit for habitation.

I In the course of her evidence, Mrs. Rylatt said the man insisted upon the baby being brought back because she would not agree to bring it up as a Roman Catholic. ' The male prisoner: There was pressure put upon me. Mr. Birchen said the photographs showed an awful contrast.

Mrs. Hibbert, who resides next door to the prisoners said she had heard the baby crying for an hour and a half at atime. She had been in the house but it was in such ' a filthy condition that she was glad to get out. Inspector Hackett, after describing the state of the children and the house, said the baby did not appear to have been washed for weeks. His opinion was that drink and mismanagement were the cause of the neglect —mismanagement and incapacity so far as the woman was concerned, and drink in the case of the man, who was always drunk at the week end. Dr. Peacocke said there was no organic disease to account for the child's condition. He saw it on Satnr- day last at the Infirmary, and it was looking better. The male prisoner said he had done his level best" for the children, according to the assistance he had had. They had never been in want of food "such as it was." Shortly after the baby was brought back it started to cut its teeth and had diarrhcea for three or four weeks. He made a mistake in taking it away from Mrs. Rylatt.
