The Mayor's Casting Vote. There was a long discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening, with reference to, the plans for the completion of the Techni- cal School Building. ' The minutes of the committee included resolutions that Mr. J. AL Murray be appointed director of educa- cation at a 'salary of £300; that the plans for the completion of the Technical School, prepared by Messrs. W. and S. Owen, be approved and submitted to the Council; that the hearty thanks of the committee be given to Mr. Vere B. Davies for his donation of works by the late William Beamont, including many with his MS. notes and additions; that the Town Clerk be requested to communicate with the executors eif the late William Beamont, and to arrange for the transfer to the Museum of the pictures bequeathed by him to the Corporation. Alderman MONKS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, called attention to the gift of Mr. • Vere B. Davies. Mr. Davies had gone out of his way to give to the Museum and Library some books which formerly belonged to the late .Mrs. Beamont. The books were not only valuable in theinsayes but much more so inasmuch as they completed certain editions which were wanting. the committee was now in possession of a complete edition of the whole of Mr. kdeamont's.works. With reference to the appointment of a director of education, the 'committee had three gentlemen before them and the committee finally selected Mr. Murray, who had had the particular kind of experience during the last eight years which seemed to qualify him for the new 'duties which he would be called upon to perform in Warrington. He had received a letter from Mr. Murray stating that he would be able to take up his duties at Warrington on Monday, the 12th inst. With regard to the plans for the completion of the Technical Institute,he would remind the Council that the present was not the first time on which the sub- ject had been brought forward. The plans ' were to. all intents and purposes passed by the Council on October 30, 1900. The plans were then really passed but it was fair and proper that they should come up Ifor re-consideration, seeing that a good deal had happened since then,and probably some members had had the details crowded out of their memory. The Alderman then went into a thorough explanation of the plans, which were displayed on the walls of the Council 'Chamber. The new buildings, he pointed out, were to be built immediately . behind the present schools, and would have a frontage to Museum-street. The buildings would be two storeys high. On the ground floor there would be a large room 601 t. by 30ft. which will be provided with partitions and could be used as one room or three small rooms. There would also be smaller class- rooms, cloak-room and lavatory accommodation, and a caretaker's house. In addition there would he an assembly hall 59 feet by 38 feet, which could be used for lectures, prize distributions, dinners, dances, and social functions. The basement could be nsed for stoeage and cooking purposes. There would be inter- communication with the Parr Hall by meams of a corridor. It was intended to use the buildings for the continuation and commercial classes which, up to the present, had been carried' on at the People's College. There were upwards of 522 students .in these classes. There was every reason to believe that the numbers would be doubled before very mubh longer. The build- ings could also be used as a higher grade elementary school, and there was no doubt that the need of such a sohool wasseverely felt in the town for boys and girls. It was computed that there were 542 boys in the upper standards of the public elementary schools,the greater part of whom ought to be having instruction in a higher grade elementary school. In providing the present accommodation they were not exceeding the immediate requirements of the town and what the committee might reasonably ask for. He believed the accommodation would be found too small in 10 or 15 years. The cost of the technical school, including furniture, was £15,000. That amount would probably be exceeded by :E.50 or IWO. Councillor DODDS : Does that sum include the price of the site. Alderman MONKS: No; that was paid for previously. Part of the land was given by the Mayor in his present- ation of Parr Hall. The estimated cost of the proposed buildings was £ll,ooo.and £5OO for the furniture. They were scarcely spending one half the amount which ether townshad spent for a like purpose. Portsmouth, which had a population something like that of Warrington. had spent £60,000 and Wigan had spent far in excess of what they were spending in Warrington. It was not necessary to decorate the proposed buildings to thesame extent as the technical school. The proposedassembly hall would seat 400 and if anyone wanted to give a dinner there it would comfortably seat 130 or 150 people. The report present to the Council suggested that the work had been considerably hampered by the want of a moderately sized assembly hall. It could be used for the distribution of prizes, for courses of lectures in connection with the schools, for the Uni- versity Extension lectures, exhibitions, parties and social gatherings amongst the students. He attached considerable importance to these social gatheries and they had a very pleasant experience on Friday last when the students had their animal soiree. The Mayoress was present and expressed her great pleasure at the way the soiree was conducted. Apart from the special use of the hall for the use of the students he thought there were certa n public uses to which it could be put. They had no hall in the possession of the Corporation between the Parr Hall and the Council Chamber that was suitable for public functions and this hall would meet that want. It would do for small meetings. The Town Clerk was often asked for a smaller hall than the Parr Hall and the proposed hall would no doubt help in the letting of the larger hall. He hoped the Council would see its way to approve of the expenditure. It would be necessary to apply to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow the money, and meanwhile he thought it was desirable that the architectshould draw up specifications and obtain tenders. One strong reason for putting it forward now, was that the preliminary work might be completed and the buildPng operations commenced in the spring, and have them completed during the best part of the year. (Hear, hear.) Councillor F.R. ROBERTS seconded the adoption of the minutes. COUpCillOr BENNETT observed that there was no man in Warrington who was more entitled to credit for his exertions on behalf of a good cause than Alderman Monks. (Hear, hear.) Notwithstanding that he (Coun- cillor Bennett) was a member of the committee, he felt bound-to move a resolution that the plans be referred back for further consideration. His objections were two-fold. In the first place the new Education Act was about to come into operation—he believed on the 26th of March next—and it would be advisable for thg Com- mittee to defer the consideration of this scheme until then, for he believed they might then provide a better scheme when they knew what they would require under the new Act. The present scheme peed not be rushed. Although their educational facilities were not all that could be desired, they would not seriously suffer by postponing the proposed extensions for a short time. 'Mr. Monks had told them that the plans had really been passed two years before. That was true as regarded the black plan, but he did not think the plans had been before the Council in their present form. For £ll,OOO they ought to get a better result than that shown. He did not wish to say anything against the eminent firm of architects who had prepared the plans,but bethought it would have been much fairer if the Corporation had asked for competitive plans and thrown the competition open to any architects who cared to compete. (Hear, hear.) The new Technical Institute was a beeautiful building, and the difference in the cost was only £2,000. Anyone who compared the two plans would be struck with the fact that for a difference of £2,000 they got a building much inferior to the bne in Palmyra-square. ;He did not pose as an architect, but he did not think the scheme was thoroughly homogenous. His second ob- jection was to the elevation itself. He did not wish to seem very critical, but he must honestly admit that when he first saw the elevation, it reminded him of a certain fustian cutting shop in Warrington with a little embellishment. (Laughter.) Councillor Bennett pro- ceeded to criticise the appearance of the building generally and considered it a defect that it was only two storeys high. Anyone approaching the building from Wilson-Patten-street would see over the roof and a hideous conglomeration of gables, spouts and back walls would meet the eye. He would have been much more reconciled to the plans if it had been a three storeyed building. He held that the Corporation ought to set the highest possible standard of taste in architecture, for if the Corporation did not build decent buildings who in the name of fortune would. (Hear, hear). In referring to the proposed hall, Councillor Bennett said it would cost £6,000 which was avery undue proportion of the whole cost. They were stinting their accommo- dation for the students in order to get a hall. Councillor PEMBERTON seconded the amendment. He did not think the hall was required. There was the gymnasium and the Parr Hall on either side of the in- stitute and he thought they could be used by the students when desired. He did not think it was an opportune time for the Corporation to spend £3,000 en a hall of that description. (Hear, hear). Councillor BURTON said he had been told that there were 1,200 scholars at People's College School and a man had recently complained to him that he could not get his child admitted.. If the school was so fully occupied in the day tithe be did not think it advisable that students should be called upon to use it at night. They needed more accommodaticn than was provided at

present for students. (Hear, hear). . I Councillor PIERPOINT said he gathered from the speech of Alderman Monks that the object of the exten- sions was to fit the school for purposes of social enter- tainment—dinners, balls and conversaziones. If the Council had decided to compete with the tradesmen of Warrington in that direction he did not envy them their ! feelings. They could do it but he should protest against I it. If the extension were required for purposes of educa- tion and they could not carry on the education without, he was prepared to vote for it, but if it was in order to suit the ideas of some visionaries who wanted

, to anticipate the wants of the town by twenty years, he I objected in toto. The whole scheme could wait. The land was the property of the Corporation and they would be able to erect such buildings as they required in twenty years if they wanted them or in ten years if they were needed. If Alderman Monks would assure him that it was absolutely necessary in order to carry out the scheme of technical education in Warrington that this immense sum of money was required he would vote for it, but not otherwise. Alderman BOLTON was of the opinion that the land had not been covered to the best advantage. With regard to the proposed extension he did not think they ought to spend the ratepayers' money in building a lot of useless rooms which would only be required once in twelve months. He contended that only the rooms absolutely necessary should be added and that the Coun- cil should carry out further details later on. They were told that the Education Act would involve a rate of sd. in the pound so that they did not want to incur useless expense. He thought they should wait and see what money would be required under the Act. With regard to the plans tenders should have been asked for from various architects, and the matter settled on a proper basis. Councillor JAMES EVANS was also of the opinion that the plans should be reconsidered by the committee who could afterwards inform the Council what was actually necessary for the carryingout of technical education,apart from the question of entertainments. Healso thought that the plans should have been open to competition. Councillor UPSON observed that if the buildings were to serve so many purposes as had been mentioned they would serve none of them efficiently. Reference had been made to the establishment of a higher grade elementary school in the build- ings but he would ask the committee to inquire whether it would not be more advisable to establish an organized school of science. A child in an organized school of science earned a grant of between £5 and £6, but a child in a higher grade elementary school did not earn more than half that amount. They would require practically the same staff and he certainly could not see that a higher grade elementary school would be self-supporting. He believed organized schools of science were self-supporting because of the higher grants they earned ' from the Im- perial Exchequer. If when the Council applied to the Local Government Board for permission to borrow the money they stated that the buildings were going to be used for the purposes of a higher grade elementary school, they might be debarred from using them as an organized school of science. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Surrox said Councillor Bennett's speech had been embellished in his usual style with high- sounding adjectives which, summed up, meant nothing more or less than sentiment—(laughter)—because he based his objection altogether upon the character of the buildings. He (the speaker) did not see that it was at all necessary for the Council to make the buildings in Museum-street in any way to compare with the build- ings in Palmyra-square. . Councillor PIEFteoiNT) Why? . . _

Alderman SUTTON: Simply-for the reason that they are two separate buildings in two different streets and when you are looking at one ydu connot see the other. (Laughter.) If that explanation is not good enough I don't know what you want. (Laughter.)

Councillor PIERPOINT It is very satisfactory. (Laughter). Alderman St:l7ON, continuing, said that if it were desirable to' have the work carried out, it would be betterto have it carried out altogether than to have it done piecemeal. He, however, was of the opinion that it was desirable to podtpone the extension for a time. Alderman SMETHURST supported the amendment. He said the Council were Asked to spend £ll,OOO on build- ings which, in his opinion, would not be required for some years to come. Theywouldbe asked at the next Council meeting to spend something like £70,000 on waterworks. These were things which kept cropping up and he was of the opinion that it ,would be better if the Council turned their attention to nearer the centre of the town, looked after the health of the people, and widened the streets. He was glad to see they were going to have Market Gate widened, and that they were making good strides towards widening one side of Bridge-street. He would like to see the money spent in a way that would do some good. That Council Cham- ber needed making two or three times larger in order that the Council and the public who attended the.meet- ings might be made more comfortable. (Hear, hear.) Councillor TINNION thought the question raised by Councillor Upson should be discussed by the Museum Committee. His (the speaker's) greatest objection to the scheme was not that the Council was providing effi- cient higher education for the children of Warrington but that thsy were providing a hall at considerable ex- pense which was not at all in keeping with the other portion of the buildings. He took it that the building would not be used simply as a hall of pleasure. It was a lamentable fact that so many children had to attend higher grade 'schools in Manchesternnd Liverpool when facilities might be provided in Warrington, Any money which was spent on providing efficient education and giving the opportunity to any child to obtain efficient education was money well-spent. (Hear, hear.) If the citizens of the next generation had the advantage of such an education they would be bettercitizens than the present generation. (Hear, hear.) Alderman MONKS, in reply, said that Councillor Tinnion gave expression to the desire that all should be done that possibly could be done in the interests of education pure and simple. That was the one point which the committee had constantly kept before them. Although he connected the proposed new rooms with social gatherings they were not designed with that i object n view. That was entirely secondary and in the back ground. The class rooms would never be used for such purposes. Whether the building was used as an organized science school or a higher grade elementary school the class rooms would serve either purpose ana had been designed with that object in view. As to Councillor Upson's suggestion, the point had not been overlooked. The committee felt the time had arrived when in order to carry out educational work with any- thing like the proper facilities and on proper lines, they ought to give the children the advantages which the • present day competition urgently demanded, and by the spending of a little more money give them the educa- tion which would enable them to compete successfully with their competitors whether of other towns or of other countries. (Hear, hear.) The class rooms were urgently required in order to complete their scheme of education which was worked out origin- ally five years ago and which they had constantly brought,before them from time to time as it had seemed desirable. All the proposed additions were in accord- ance with that scheme. The committee thought that if the buildings could be let for social gatherings it might possibly be a source of income. As to the urgency of the rooms, the work of the committee had been very greatly hampered during the past few years by classes having to meet in People's College. The conditions there were not what they should be. The rooms were too dark and there was no means of providing the necessary supervision. If the classes were removed to the new buildings, they would be brought under the control of the new director. of education and into harmony with the technical school which was an entirely separate institution from the buildings which it was proposed to erect. The new buildings would be a sort of preparing ground for the students who were moving on to the technical school which gave a higher form of education. As regarded the hall and basement he did not mind leaving that portion of the scheme over for further consideration if the Council desired. With- out the hall and basement the cost of the scheme would be about £5,500. In reply to Councillor Bennett, the speaker pointed out that that gentleman strongly object- ed to the plans for the technical school, but now he had lived long enough to withdraw all his criticisms and to express his warm admiration of the build- ing. He (Alderman Monks) had no hesitation , in saying that. the same result would come ,about in regard to the new buildings. Alderman Monks replied at length to Councillor Bennett's criticisms. He emphasised the fact that the ornamentation of a building should be adapted to the purpose for which it would be used, and the committee thought that the new buildings when completed would be a great improve- ment on most buildings in Warrington at the present time. The two buildings could not be seen from ' one , position and he therefore thought the elevation should be considered satisfactory. The proposal that the buildings should be concentrated under one roof was absurd. With regard to Councillor Bennett 's statement as to the view of the gables &c., from Museum-street, I the building stood 58 feet from the street and could only be seen through an opening which was 18 feet wide. I I A pair of solid wooden gates would be erected at the open- ing. With regard to the attendance at People's College day tshc he oaotlt,etahtei eßn o ea rf dt hoefmEada au cgaetri so nt to hd eq fnai ct et rtehcaetn tt hl ye called aver- age attendance was in exces.4 of the legal number of places in the school and that would account for children not being admitted. Certainly it did not seem to him desirable that instruction should go on in the day time and that the students at the evening classes should have to occupy the rooms in the evening. On a vote being taken thirteen voted for the nmend- Trent and thirteen for the resolution. The MAYOR gave his casting vote in favour of the amendment and consequently the proposal . is referred back to the committee for further consideration. •

div.head: Recent Eisteddfod.
div.p: The Recent Eisteddfod.

Sir,—We hope we may rely upon your kind indulgence to allow us to reply on this correspondence. We would point out to begin with that the anonymous gentleman (Mr. S. Hassall), whom we managed to get out of hiding place, is Mr. Payton's deputy-conductor. The other two gentlemen have not come forth, but we venture to say that, even if both letters don't emanate from, they are inspired by members of Mr. Payton's choir. So that your readers will be able to perceive that the "interest" that is so gratifying to him is an engineered interest." • Our interest has been compulsory, and we cannot think that he includes us in his gratification, as every single point he has raised we have completely swept away. The forlorn hope he hangs on to is not the point he contended for. in his first letter, as after making certain insinua- tions and allegations he said " At these choir competi- tions, the choirs should in my opinion consist of bona- fide members." We addressed ourselves to this and re- ceived a grave and certain answer, then he changes his ground and it now appears that what he really required Nyasa residental certificate. It is perhaps only fair to the winning choir that weshould give the nature of the assurance above mentioned. It is as. follows :—That the members complained of are on the books, have paid the usually weekly subscription, and have attended the rehearsals and we, as an Eisteddfod committee, would have no 'Agitation in again holding that their bona- fides are beyond reproach. The words of the statement that Mr. Berrey has something to do with getting up the Eisteddfod are plain English (considering that he had a great deal to do with getting up the "Eisteddfod") and cannot be misread, and this as we pointed out in our first letter was what Mr. Payton was then insinuating and is the cause of the whole matter. He replies to Mr. Berrey that he doesn't mean what he says and is sorry that Mr. Berrey so reads it. He doesn't reply or express any sorrow to us aud we are left to assume from the nature of his reply that it was only at this committee that the allegation was directed. We say to him you know the statement is untrue, be manly, withdraw it. We are not going to waste ink on the other gentleman but with your kind permission we should like to give your readers some idea of what this Eisteddfod has meant for us and why we have shirked nothing in this correspondence. The Apollo Choir consists of about 40 young men, none of whom are too well blest with this worlds goods, but who willingly gave their time and trouble. The prizes we gave and the expenses together totalled a sum of about .280 so that it is plain to be seen that we stood to Jose something without the possibility of gaining much, and had it not proved a success each of us might have had to give something in addition to time and trouble. It being a modest start and something new for Warring- ton we were quite satisfied to make it pay, and are pleased to say that it has just done so. It is our inten- tion to run it as an annual affair and we think that we are entitled to ask for encouragement and not hostility from the musical profession. We had hundreds of entries and the incentive to study and to et the best professional tuition will be such that those in the musi- cal profession are bound to benefit. As a result of the Eisteddfod we hear that another male choir is being formed and this alone is sufficient indication of the interest that we have aroused. We shall not be dis- couraged by hostile criticism, but we resent and shall resent any imputations of unfairness. We went into the Eisteddfod and came out of it with clean hands and a clean conscience and we can conscientiously say that there is not a man on this committee who would have tolerated anything that was not straight. The movement is, in our humble opinion a good one and in the best interests of music, and we have felt that it would have been a mistake to have ignored these insinuation and allegations, directed against the committee controlling it and to have done so would have been to allow it to be wrecked at the outset.

Thanking you Mr. Editor for your e4treme courtesy in allowing us to monopolise so much of your valuable space. We remain, yours sincerely, THE COMMITTEE OF THE APOLLO PRIZE CHOIR. R. W. COOK, (Hon. Sec.) .
31, Selby-street, Warrington. Bth, January. 1903.

div.head: PADGATE. •
div.p: PADGATE. •

THE PAROCHIAL TEA.—Success attended the annual parochial tea meeting in connection with Christ Church, Padgate, which was held on Tuesday evening. About 160 persons sat down to tea, provided under the superin- tendence of Mrs. Grounds and Miss Bovrering and a band of workers. The Vicar announced that the new infants' school, which is almost completed, would be open for inspection while the rooni was cleared, and many availed themselves of the privilege. At the out- set of the concert the Vicar, who presided, gave a brief resume of the work of the church in the parish during the past twelve months, especially mentioning the re- decoration of the church at a cost of nearly £lOO, and the building of an infants school at a cost of £625, towards which about £525 has already been raised. The programmt opened with a mandoline quartette by Mrs. Adamson and the Misses Atkinson, Carlyle and F. Carlyle. 'After this a number of" living pictures "were presented, some of which were accompanied by musical items rendered by Mrs. Jennings, following which Captain F. M. Appleton reci- ted " King Robert of Sicily " in excellent style. The second half of the programme opened With a farce entitled "A Pair of Lunatics," the characters being sus- tained in capital style by Miss Lily Birtles and Mr. B. Riggall. Captain Appleton recited "Fuzzy Wuzzy," and living pictures were then shewn representing a num- ber of well-known pictorial advertisements, following which was a grand tableau representing "England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales." A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the artistes, on the motion of the churchwardens, Messrs. G. Mather and J. D. Buckton.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Buckley-street P.S.A.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Buckley-street P.S.A.

An open meeting in connection with the above Society was held in Buckley-street Methodist Free Church on Sunday and was well attended. Mr. W. Spruce occupied the chair, and "Owd Jeff" (Mr. J. Atherton, of Wigan) was the speaker. Mr. N. Cook tastefully rendered "Ye that are weary" and "Lead, kindly Light," and Mr. R. Cook gaveapleasing rendition of "The Sailor's Grave" and "Faith." The accom- panist was Mr. Albert E. Trow.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
By " Ovalist."

Warrington might have started the new year worse. There is, at least, that consolation available after last Saturday's match. A year ago Warrington received such a severe trouncing on New Year's day by Brad- ford as to take all the starch out of them for some time., This year they were without engagement—perhaps fortunately—on new Year's Day, and the first match of 1903 took place on Saturday, when Swinton were tbe visitors. Neither side was at full strength but the Blues were the worst sufferers from absentees and did well to draw the game. Warrington, of course, did correspondingly badly,' and there is no doubt that a team with any pretensions to class about it,should have defeated Swinton under the circumstances with ease.

The failure to do so is all the more regrettable as the Blues are 'gradually improving their record against Warrington. Time was,when it was hopeless for them to hope to win at Wilderspool, but of late years,they have generally obtained a point or two on the erstwhile fatal sward. It was in 1898-1899 season they improved and "halved" the points with the home team, each side scoring a try. Since then Warring- ton haVe been unable to regain their old time power, as the following record shows. At Swinton also the "Blues "have always held the upper hand, and in the " draw " season the "Lions" won at home by two goals two tries to nothing. In 1899-1900,at Swinton, the home team won by two tries to one try, and at Warrington the visitors were again successful by a try to a goal. In 1900-1901 season a try to nothing victory for the Blues was the verdict at Warrington, and one goal three tries to nothing at Swinton. Last season in the first year of the Northern League, the " Wirepullers " were defeated twice by Swinton, at home by a try to nothing,and at Swinton by one goal two tries to two trio's. This season the team opened on the Swinton ground, but were defeated by twelve points to nothing. For five seasons the "Wirepullers" have failed both at home and at Swinton.

The result on Saturday was bitterly disappointing. Home matches have, been so scarce this season, and points ditto, that it was hoped and believed a great effort would result in Swinton's overthrow. I don't doubt that the great effort was made—but the makinc, of it ! weltit beggars description. Warrington prob 7 ably never played worse, and few less interesting games have been seen on the Warrington ground. The conditions were not ideal, certainV, the ground being very soft and the ball greasy, but these things do not account for the wretched combination and childish efforts of the home team. Swinton "adapted themselves to the conditions far better,and had Warrington shown even as much smartness as their opponents—and it was not much—they must have won. The backs played atrociously, and have not shaped worse at scoring this season. Passin,, -was completely at sea,and Swinton were never in reafdanger. The defence of the homesters was, however,excellent,and. to this they owe the fact that they were not beaten. Swinton came very near doing the trick more than once, and Preston's failure to kick two easy goals was a lucky thing for Warrington.

To begin with, Swinton liad the wind behind them and they kept Warrington busy. Numerous efforts were. made to find an opening for Lewis, the famous sprinter, but Fish was always a match for him, and kept him at bay in a manner which showed what he could and should have done at Huddersfield. Lewis likewise kept a close eye on Fish but was several times eluded by the "artful dodger," who, however, never had much chance of scoring. In the second half Burgess and Dickenson both made great efforts to cross the line but were foiled,and Swinton carried the game to the other end. Fish had a shot at goal from the same position as Preston, but was no more successful, and a sdries of ineffectual and uninteresting scrums came to an end with the score sheet still blank.

Swinton were without R. Valentine and the regular halves, Morgan and Samuel, but the substitutes acquitted themselves well. Williamson and Critch were really smart at half, and quite out-shone the Warring- ton pair, who did nothing right, if we except one fine breakaway by Hockenhall which deserved a score. How many times has Hockenhall got through like this and found himself unsupported at the critical moment.? The Warrington half backs are playing badly, there is no doubt, aud a change, if only temporary, is neces- sary. Isherwood was badly missed, for Hallam did little on the attack, though he excelled in defective tactics. Knight was moderate at full back, and the forwards just about held their own.
The League table up to date is as follows : For Agst.

Warrington's position—only sixth from the bottom —must be seriously considered. The club is in, posi- tive danger, and unless there is a considerable im- provement in the play of the team, Warrington may find themselves in unwelcome company. I don't really anticipate anything so, dismal,especially with the big lot of home matches on the list, but a change of some kind is absolutely necessary. Just now the team is disgracing itself weekly.

Broughton Rangers at last head the table. Hull Kingston Rovers unexpectedly defeated Halifax, and the Rangers were immediately "one up." They have a better recorfl than their Yorkshire rivals, who may yet be passell by both Swinton and Salford. The latter are going very strongly just now and completely wiped the floor with Hunslet at Parkside, Lomas himself scoring ten points. The annual Mersey " Derby " came off at Widnes, where the locals just beat Runcorn by a try to nothing, and are conse- quently well pleased with themselves. The fixture, of course, counted in the South West Lancashire Com- petition.
The South-West Lancashire League table up-to-date is as follows : • Points

T rather fancy that there will be few County matchel on Saturdays after this season. The clubs who supply the men to the County team have suffered so much in their league engagements as a consequence of County calls that they are not,likely toput up with the annoy-. ance much longer. To-day Warrington have to supply, Fish, Dickenson and Boardman to the TAncashire team against Cumberland, and at the same time play Brighouse Rangers at T3righonse. Bronghton Rangers, who have only just got to the head of the League have to supply their four best backs and a forward and play Hull at Hull in addition. • Like Warrington they are Drett,7 sure to lose and the prospect is not pleas- ant for either club. The Rangers might easily lose the championship through it.

Warrimiton have keen compelled to make a big alteration in their team for to-day's match. Burgess has been dropned and Hunter promoted to the position of half while Bailey also gets a chance. The team will be : -Knight, full back; Bailey, Edmunds, Hallam, and Harris, threequarters ; Hockenhall. and Hunter, half-backs; Morrison, J, Swift; W. Swift, Cunningham, Harmer, Naylor, Edmondson and Roberts, forwards.

Noting that and are . champions of the League. The deceased was 61 year old, and had worked Hunter being very smart at half, while the three- during the day at Summerseat. quarters all tackled well. Swinton had Valentine, i
Morgan, and Cooper playing, so that additional lustre is added to Warrington "A. " performance. Hunter scored the winning point with a drop-kick.
Isherwood is working again- and his injured leg improving nicely. Tt is expected that he will be able to turn out against St. Helens next Saturday.

div.p: LOCAL TRADES UNIONISM. Town Council and Municipal Bowling
Greens.
There was a good attendance of delegates at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council which was held in the Cairo-street schools on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. Edwardson presided.

div.head: VISITS TO THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: VISITS TO THE WORKHOUSE.

The SECRETARY again raised the question of the Board of Guardians' refusal to allow a deputation from the Trades Council to visit the Workhouse periodlcally. He said that in regard to the question the Council would remember that a similar application Made by the Earles- town Trades Council' was also refused. The secretary of the Earlestown Trades Council had not, however, allowed the mater to drop, but had written to the Local Government Board asking them if there was any statute which prevented the members of the Board of Guardians granting the application which had been made for per- mission to allow a committee to visit the workhouse. He had received a reply to the effect that there was no statute which gave them power to grant the applica- tion. A further application, as to whether there was a statute which prevented them giving the permission, was answered by the secretary Of the Fabian Society, who said that he did not know of any statute. What he would advise the Trades Council to do, however, would be to get two "ratepayers to make an application, as private persons, to the Board of Guardians for permis- sion to visit the workhouse. He did not think such a request would be refused and the two appointed could then report to the Trades Council. The council decided not to take any immediate action and the matter was allowed to drop. THE UNEMPLOYED AT WARRINGTON.

The SECRETARY reported that in accordance with in- structions he had written to Mr. Robert Pierpoint,M.P., to the Town Clerk, and to Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Board of Guardians in regard to the question of the unemployed. Mr. Guardians, Pierpoint had replied to say that he could not attend to the question just then as he was about to be married. The Town Clerk had acknow- ledged the receipt of the letter which he said would be laid before the meeting of the General Purposes Com- mittee. Mr. .T. C. Sutton had also replied stating that the matter would be brought before the Board of Guardians at their next meeting. He, however, went further and stated that the only action the Board could take, was• by the administration of relief. He suggested that as a remedy for the distress they should take steps to bring about the provision of some public work, at fair wages if practicable, by the local authorities. That would be a good and at the same time a useful way of meeting the difficulty, and would not be so objectionable as the remedy of the administration of poyr-law relief. The Town Clerk had sent a further reply asking the Council for instances of the extent of the hardships endured by the working classes through want of employment. He (Mr. Stott) replied to that letter to the effect that it would be impossible for the Trades Council to obtain full information as to the extent of the dis- tress in Warrington, as the large bulk of those out of employment were not members of trades unions. They desired the Town Council to obtain the information through their officials and to formulate some scheme whereby the distress could be relieved without the persons receiving such relief being disfran- chised. He (the Secretary) had also written to Coun- cillor Upson. the secretary of the Teachers' Association asking him if the members of the Association could gain any information regarding the number of the un- employed in the town. Councillor Upson replied stat- ing that the Teacher's' Association had decided that they could not undertake to procure the information as any action on their part inthat direction might be mis- understood by the parents of the children who were questioned regarding the matter. He, however, would promise them that he would supply any information which he personally obtained. Mr, Stott here remarked that their application to the Board of Guardians had met with the fate which generally awaited their applica- t ons.

Mr. BUCKLEY said that since the question was raised at their last meeting he had taken the trouble to make inquiries as to the extent of the distress which existed in the building trade, and had found that the number of men out of work was greatly more than 25 per cent. The building trade was exceptionally bad, in fact he had never known it to be so bad.

Mr. FLAN-N.7EBx said that despite the fact that dis • tress existed in so many trades some manufacturers were working over-time and the men were putting in 80 or 90 hours ,each week. They could talk abo it their eight hours day but he did not see where it came in. He knew one case where one man was doing two men's work. Considering the number of men who were out of work he thought that it was a disgrace that such things existed, and there was something radically -ovrong with the system which allowed such things to exist. Wit.. STOTT suggested that he be insttuctkl to supply whatever informatiOn he Could to the Town Clerk. Mr. PODMORE moved that each delegate be instruc- ted to supply the Secretary with information respecting the distress which existed in the branch which he repre- sented, and that Mr, Stott forward any such information to the Town Clerk. The proposition was put to the meeting and unani- mously carried. MUNICIPAL BOWLING GREENS.

_ Mr. PODMORE, in accordance with the notice he gave at the last meeting, raised the question of the Council being called upon to provide municipal • bowling greens. The question was raised in the Council some years ago and the Town Council were then asked to pro- vide bowling greens. As was usual the Council asked them for information, and their secretary had by con- siderable trouble supplied the information. The ques- tionhad since then been lost in—the bog he called it at the last meeting—what he would now call a swamp, the General Purposes Committee,and they had heard nothing of it since. Last monthohe mentioned that there was a certain lawn, the property of the Corporation, which was used by the Corporation officials and their daughters and wives, the aldermen and councillors and their daughters and wives, to play tennispn. He thought that if they could provide lawns for that purpose they could provide bowling greens for the workingmen. The Town Council had spent some £30,000 on a police ?mind- ing wherein to deal with these people who got into trouble, and yet they refused to spend the money which would be required to provide public bowling greens, which would assist to keep the people out of trouble. It was the duty of the Town Council to provide reason- able facilities for the people of the town to obtain recreation. At present the men, women and children of the town could only obtain that recreation at the public- house or in the streets. They had in Latchford a large park, how many years they had had it he did not remem- ber, in which there was a large field used as a playground for children. He did, not say anything against that, but he thought that there was plenty of room there for the provision of a bowling green. Then there would be some land at the corner of Springfield-street, which could be made into a bowling green. He moved that the Council be again asked to take into consideration the question of the provision of municipal bowling greens. Mr. BUCKLEY seconded, and Mr. YORK supported the proposition which was unanimously carried. FAIR CONTRACTS. Mr. Bucitt,Ev stated that he had sonic information regarding the fair contracts question. He moved that the secretary be instructed to write to the Town Clerk as soon as he (the speaker) had verified the information and placed it in the secretary's hands. MORE MUNICIPAL MATTERS. Mr. FLANNERY gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the Trades Council give ,an expression of opinion as to whether the Town Council should re- build and retain those public houses which they had to purchase in order to effect public improvements. He would also move that the Town Council be asked to consider the erection of an annexe to the Museum to be used as a smoke room and a writing room. He would further move that the Town Council be requested to consider ,the question of a reduction of the fees charged at the baths.

A Painful Mistake. A. painful case was investigated by Mr. Brighouse. coroner of St. Helens on Monday. A Mrs. Joseph Swift, a very respectable woman, went to Visit some friends on New Year's Day,and started for home about ten o'clock. An hour later a party of young men near Leach's-lane, saw Mrs. Swift, who was a stranger to them, lying in the roadway. They asked her what she was doing there, and she replied, apparantly somewhatniuddled, that she Was waiting for her husband. Thinking she was drunk, they earriod her on to the footpath, and left her there, and during the night she died of exposure.—Dr. Unsworth informed the jury that there was not the slightest trace of alcohol in the woman's body, and that the primary cause of death was the sudden breaking of a ,small blood-vessel iir the brain.

Developments on the Nile Valley Gold Company's property at Um Gam iart, about 60 miles from Assouan, are being watched with keen interest. From the mine manager's reports (which are said to be confirmed from independent sources) it is considered probable that a new goldfield is being opened up in Egypt that will add materially to the world's supply of that precious metal. —" Financial News," January 8.

div.head: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S WORKS. Action for Compensation.
div.p: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S WORKS. Action for Compensation.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday before his Honour Judge, Bowen Rowlands, K.C., a claim was heard under the Workmen's Compensation Act arising out of an accident at Messrs. Crosfleld's works in which a carter in the employ of Mr. Isherwood, contactor,. named Richard Rawlinson fell on a drum and injured. his ribs, from, which injury he 'died some time after- wards. The applicant was Mary Catherine Rawlinson daughter of the deceased,now residing with her brother at Folkestone and her claim was for 156 compensation and .210 medical and burial expenses.—Mr. Rigby Swift (instructed by Mr. H. J. Longton) represented the appli- cant, Mr. Elliott (instructed by Mr. Unsworth) appeared for Mr. Isherwood, the contractor) ' • Mr. J. F. Byrne (instructed by Mr. Richard Evans) defended the case on bacilli of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, and Mt.. Unsworth represented Mr. Newton, who had beeni brought in as a third party to the action. Mr. Swift stated the plaintiff's case at considerable length, and pointed out that the respondents (Messrs. Crosfields and Sons) in their answers which they had put in asserted that the deceased was not immediately employed by them in work which was ancillary or in- cidental to the business carried on, and that therefore they were not undertakers within the meaning of the Act. The respondents also contended that the deceased left no dependents within the meaning of the Act. Mr. Swift urged that the respondents were undertakers within tha meaning of the Act inasmuch as the deceased was engaged in carrying stuff from their factory to the wharf.

Mr. Byrne said he Accepted Mr. Swift's view that the respondents were undertakers Within the meaning of the Act. His acceptance of that view would reduce the i ssue to one of whether the applicant was a dependent within the meaning of the act. Mr. Swift. in explaining the applicant's Position, said up to three years ago the deceased had a house at Lymm and the applicant lived with him and was entirely de- pendent upon him. It was decided that she should learn dressmaking and for that purpose she went to her brother's at Folkestone. The deceased broke up his house, stored his furniture and went to live in lodgings at Warrington. Whilst his daughter was at Folkestone he sent her sums of money. He (Mr. Swift) could not suggest that for the whole of the last three years, the deceased had entirely _ supported her. She had had assistance from. other relatives but he could not say how much. She was in delicate health and unable to travel from Folkestone. ' Robert Rawlinson, son of the deceased, gave evidence In support of Counsel's statement and stated that on. three occasions he had seen his father send money to sister at Folkestone.—Cross-examined by Mr. Byrne, witness said his father received a legacy of £lOO from a son who diedti. few years ago. He had this money when he sent contributions to thy applicant. Mr. Byrne argued that there was no evidence that the. applicant was dependent upon the deceased. There was no legal liability upon the deceased to maintain this. daughter after she had attained her majority and that was before she went to Folkestone. She could not com- pel her father to support her; that could only be done. by virtue of the poor laws. Mr. Swift contended that the Act of Parliament made no distinction. The Act dealt with members of a family. who were wholly or part dependent. Mr. Byrne said it was not enough to prove that she was dependent upon gifts from her father but that she Wag dependent upon his earnings at the time of his. death.
His Honour said he sympathised with Mr. Swift in the position he was in, but at the same time he should find very great difficulty in finding in his favour on the evidence given. _ _

Mr. Swift said he could not help feeling that in the absence of the applicant he was in a great, di diculty. After a brief consultation with Mr. Byrne. Mr, Swift said he did not think it was worth while asking for an anjournment in order that the applicant might be present. He would therefore not proceed with that part of the claim, and he would now ask for funeral expenses allowed by the Ace. Mr. Byrne had met him very fairly and had agreed to an award in theapplicant's favour for £lO funeral expenses and .£5 costs. His Honour entered judgment for this amount. Mr. Elliott applied for his costs from the respondents. who had brought hinfin as a third party. His Honour allowed costs on the brief and counsel's fee and also allowed Mr. Unsworth his cost against the respondents.

A HORSE DEFIES A REMOUNT DEPARTMENT.—The wild Mexican horse that for over three weeks has eluded the pursuit of the Colchester garrison was seized on Tuesday, but once more escaped. The officer command- ing the remount department at Colchester having offered a reward for the capture of the animal, three cavalry soldiers rode over to the village of Messing, which the horse had selected 'as its headquarters, and chased it over the fields and threw the woods. One man succeeded in riding it down. and having seized its inane he was about to slip-a collar over its head when the animal reared, and striking him violently with one of its fore- legs again got away. At sunset the soldiers had driven the horse into a park on the estate of Mr. James Round, M.P., where it was still roaming about. A collecting . clerk of the Claude Lofontaine Bank, Paris,ha.s been robbed of 50,000 francs (says a "Standard" telegram.) The man .was collecting a large sum at the cashier's department of the Louvre dry goods stores. Suddenly two persons warned him that he had dropped a five-franc piece. As he had heard a coin ring the clerk bent down to see which way it had rolled. Whilst doing so the thieves extracted a roll .of notes from his open portfolio which he had left on the counter, and were able to decamp before an alarm could be raised. Further evidence was given at Southwarkf(London) Police Court on Wednesday against George Chapman, alais Severino lilowsowski, until recently a publican, and formerly of Warsaw, a Prussian Pole, on'the charges of murdering Maud Marsh, Mary Isabella Spink, and Elizabeth Taylor. Before the prisoner was placed in the dock he was identified by hit,' Polish wife and sister-in-law.

THE FARM ROBBERY AT SANKEY—OFFENDERS SENT TO GAOL-At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Colonel J. C. RidgwayandMr, F. A. Frost, John Jackson. 33, Elizabeth-street, and William Smith, Selby-street, were sent to gaol for three months for stealing, between the 18th and 19th December, nine ducks, four turkeys, four geese, thirtythens and two tame rabbits, valued at 10s., the property of William. Taylor' farmer, Brow Farm, Sankey,—Evidence was again given to the effect that the fowls and rabbits were stolen during the night and on December 19th Smith sold the rabbits to Jonathan Broadhurst, greengrocer, Bostock-street for two shillings. Broadhurst,was also asked to buy some fowls but refused.

RUGBY FOOTBALL. ----- FRIENDLY MATCH. RU.NCORN "A " v. LATCHFORD RANGERS.—These, teams met on the Runcorn ground on Saturday, before a moderate attendance of spectators. The game ended in a pointless draw. LANCASHIRE COMBINATION. . WARRINGTON "A" DEFEAT SWINTON. Warrington "A" visited ' Swinton on Saturday and gained a victory by a goal to nil. The visiting team was not up to its usual strength, and this makes the re- sult all the more creditable. The early phases of the match went in favour of the visitors, Fillingham in particular showing fine form. The smart work of the visiting forwards constantly harms:3pd the home custodian, and twice in quick succession Wood was tackled in possession. A fine run by Bailey was a feature during the first half, and Swinton were a lucky• team to cross over at half-time with no tangible score. recorded against them. During the second half the, Warringtonians again asserted themselves, and brilliant work by Duckworth and Hunter maintained the nggre- sive. • A fine dropped goal by Hunter settled the issue, of the match, and Warrington thus won by • two points o nil. New York has recently been treated to a series of ' sensational crimes of increasing barbarity. On Wed- nesday there occured a tragedy that marks a climax in atrocity. In the Mount Vernon home of John Finlay, a New 'York millionaire business man and head of the' Saks Company department store, a recently-dismissed coachman called to propose marriage to a housemaid. The latter jeered at the proposal, and he pursued her - into the house. Passing through the drawing-room,he saw Finlay's only child, a little flaxen-haired girl,. seated on a mound of cushions turning the pages of a picture-book. Seizing her by the hair he raised her in. the air, and with a razor severed her head. Failing to. reach the housemaid, he blew his own brains out. Both of the child's parents are almost insane with grief. REX TONNEA r G H.P. MOTOR. CAR, second-hand,. equal to new.—Apply J. S. GARLAND, Motor Car Depot, 51,53, St 55, 13ridge-st.,Warrington.—Advt.
